title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
應天府鄉試錄序
嘉靖甲午秋右諭德臣以訓左賛
善臣治恭承
上命來主應天鄉試臣以訓竊伏自念
臣海濱之野人也敢與知都人
士之文事矧進退是司或則譬
之曰延陵季子之聘上國也見
===
四代之樂與諸國之風而能一
言其故子自越觀于江淮其諸
吳之之魯也乎勉之何辭臣曰
諾哉如期而至提調則府尹臣
奇府丞臣登庸院宇廓新百需整
裕臣曰僉其樂有寧宇以共夙
夜乎監試則御史臣英臣宜綜

應天府鄉試錄序
嘉靖甲午秋右諭德臣翁訓左賛
善臣治恭承
上命來主應天鄉試臣翁訓竊伏自念
臣海濱之野人也敢與知都人
士之文事矧進退是司或則譬
之曰延陵季子之聘上國也〔□〕
===
四代之樂與諸國之風而能一
言其故子自越觀于江淮其諸
吳之之魯也乎勉之何辭臣曰
諸哉如期而至提調則府尹臣
奇府丞臣登庸院宇廓新百需整
裕臣曰僉其樂有寧宇以共夙
夜乎監試則御史臣英臣宜綜
punctuated:
應天府鄉試錄序

嘉靖甲午秋，右諭德臣以訓、左賛善臣治，恭承上命，來主應天鄉試。臣以訓竊伏自念：臣海濱之野人也，敢與知都人士之文事？矧進退是司！或則譬之曰：「延陵季子之聘上國也，見四代之樂與諸國之風，而能一言其故。子自越觀于江淮，其諸吳之之魯也乎？勉之，何辭！」臣曰：「諾哉！」如期而至。提調則府尹臣奇、府丞臣登庸，院宇廓新，百需整裕。臣曰：「僉其樂有寧宇以共夙夜乎！」監試則御史臣英、臣宜，綜
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the autumn of the jiawu year of Jiajing [1534], your servants Yixun, Right Exhorter, and Zhi, Left Admonisher, respectfully received Your Majesty’s command and came to preside over the Yingtian Provincial Examination. I, your servant Yixun, privately reflected with trepidation: I am an uncultivated man from the seacoast. How could I presume to judge the literary work of the capital’s scholars, much less take charge of advancing or rejecting them!

Someone offered this analogy: “When Jizi of Yanling visited the upper states as an envoy, he witnessed the music of the four dynasties and the Airs of the various states, and could explain the significance of each in a single remark. You have come from Yue to observe the region of the Yangzi and Huai rivers: is this not like that man of Wu’s journey to Lu? Apply yourself! Why decline?” Your servant replied, “Very well!”

We arrived at the appointed time. The Proctors were your servants Qi, Prefect, and Dengyong, Vice Prefect. The examination compound was spacious and newly refurbished, and all necessary supplies were duly prepared and abundant. Your servant said, “Surely everyone will rejoice in having peaceful quarters in which to attend to their duties morning and night!” The officials overseeing the examination were your servants Ying and Yi, Investigating Censors, who coordinated …

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
練周防豫事有嚴臣曰士其獲
見所長乎同考試則教授臣軒
學正臣淮教諭臣瑞葵臣祚臣子麟
臣獻忠臣永壽臣煦訓導臣鵬先期
應聘至皆四方之良也臣曰重
任其有所分乎提學御史臣聞
人詮暨六館諸曹之長各慎擇
===
===
所蒞士以待事凡三千六百有
奇臣曰士其既簡矣乎乃如制
三試三校之錄士百三十有五
人梓其文二十篇登于
天府臣惟樂者聲諸器者也言者聲
諸心者也聲諸器傳諸人聽之
而得其情與其風之美惡祚之

奇臣曰士其旣簡矣乎乃如制
三試三校之錄士百三十有五
人梓其文二十篇登于
天府臣惟樂者聲諸器者也言者聲
諸心者也聲諸器傳諸人聽之
而得其情與其風之美惡祚之
punctuated:
練周防，豫事有嚴。臣曰：「士其獲見所長乎？」同考試則教授臣軒、學正臣淮、教諭臣瑞葵、臣祚、臣子麟、臣獻忠、臣永壽、臣煦、訓導臣鵬，先期應聘至，皆四方之良也。臣曰：「重任其有所分乎？」提學御史臣聞人詮暨六館諸曹之長，各慎擇所蒞士以待事，凡三千六百有奇。臣曰：「士其既簡矣乎？」乃如制三試三校之，錄士百三十有五人，梓其文二十篇，登于天府。
臣惟樂者，聲諸器者也；言者，聲諸心者也。聲諸器，傳諸人，聽之而得其情與其風之美惡、祚之
translation_en:
…experienced and thorough in their precautions, they made strict preparations for the proceedings. Your servant said: “Will the candidates now have the opportunity to display their strengths?” The Associate Examiners were Professor Xuan, School Instructor Huai, Instructors Ruikui, Zuo, Zilin, Xianzhong, Yongshou, and Xu, and Assistant Instructor Peng—all your servants. They accepted their appointments and arrived before the appointed date; all were outstanding men from the four quarters. Your servant said: “May this weighty responsibility now be shared?” The Education Censor, your servant Wenren Quan, together with the heads of the six colleges and the various bureaus, each carefully selected the scholars under their supervision to take part in the examination: more than three thousand six hundred in all. Your servant said: “Have the candidates now been duly selected?” Accordingly, following the regulations, we examined them in three sessions and assessed their work three times, selecting one hundred and thirty-five men. Twenty of their compositions were printed from woodblocks and submitted to the imperial archives.
Your servant reflects that music gives sound through instruments, while speech gives sound to the heart. What is sounded through instruments is transmitted to others; by listening, one can apprehend its sentiments, the goodness or badness of its customs, and its allotted fortune’s …

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
升降況夫聲諸心者由中應外
誠之不可揜也孰謂聽焉而無
得也哉彼都人士出言有章是
我
國家百餘年豐芑之遺而我
聖天子作人之功之所先施
嚮明之化之所先被故夫覩山川
===
之鉅麗而占靈秀之委閱人文
之炳蔚而仰
聖澤之深治世之聲其將是在乎或
則又曰聲之未被於樂者自然
之聲也節奏短長之而大音或
幾乎散矣言之未約於文者由
衷之言也組繪離合之而心聲

嚮明之化之所先被故夫覩山川
之鉅麗而占靈秀之委閱人文
===
之炳蔚而仰
聖澤之深洽世之聲其將是在乎哉
則又曰聲之未被於樂者自然
之聲也節奏短長之而大音或
幾乎散矣言之未約於文者由
衷之言也組繪離合之而心聲
punctuated:
升降。況夫聲諸心者，由中應外，誠之不可揜也，孰謂聽焉而無得也哉？彼都人士，出言有章，是我國家百餘年豐芑之遺，而我聖天子作人之功之所先施，嚮明之化之所先被。故夫覩山川之鉅麗而占靈秀之委，閱人文之炳蔚而仰聖澤之深，治世之聲，其將是在乎？
或則又曰：「聲之未被於樂者，自然之聲也；節奏短長之，而大音或幾乎散矣。言之未約於文者，由衷之言也；組繪離合之，而心聲
translation_en:
…rise and decline. How much more so with what finds voice in the heart: it proceeds from within and responds outwardly, and its sincerity cannot be concealed. Who could say that one hears it without gaining any understanding? Those gentlemen of the capital speak with refinement. This is the legacy of more than a hundred years of our dynasty’s abundant cultivation of talent. Here our sagely Son of Heaven’s efforts to nurture men have first been applied, and the transforming influence of his enlightened rule has first been received. Thus, beholding the grandeur and beauty of the mountains and rivers, one discerns where their spiritual excellence gathers; surveying the brilliant richness of literary accomplishment, one looks up in admiration at the depth of imperial beneficence. Might the sounds of a well-governed age be found here?
Yet someone else says: “Sounds not yet set to music are natural sounds. Regulate them with rhythm and measure, lengthening and shortening them, and the great sound may almost be dissipated. Words not yet constrained into literary form are words from the heart. Embellish them with woven patterns and painted colors, separating and combining them, and the heart’s voice…”

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
或幾乎隱矣是故知言知樂古
人難之子既有得矣乎臣不佞
乃何敢望古人亦惟仰體
聖天子崇雅抑浮之德意推而行之
惟其明理致用無或騖於玄虛
惟其通古今之宜無或眩博以
逞惟其深厚爾雅無或夸毗儇
===
佻徒取觀聽以若所言揆若所
志持吾鑑空衡平之心以順應
乎其間雖不悉中亦思過半焉
視諸審樂知德者不既有間矣
乎臣今也幸而蒙成於百執事
且將億之曰庶幾其有名世者
出是舉焉俾臣幸復蒙成于將

佻徒取觀聽以若所言揆若所
志持吾鑑空衡平之心以順應
乎其間雖不悉中亦思過半焉
視諸審樂知德者不既有間矣
乎臣今也幸而蒙成於百執事
且將億之曰庶幾其有名世者
出是舉焉俾臣幸復蒙成于將
punctuated: 或幾乎隱矣。是故知言知樂，古人難之。子既有得矣乎？臣不佞，乃何敢望古人？亦惟仰體聖天子崇雅抑浮之德意，推而行之：惟其明理致用，無或騖於玄虛；惟其通古今之宜，無或眩博以逞；惟其深厚爾雅，無或夸毗儇佻，徒取觀聽。以若所言，揆若所志，持吾鑑空衡平之心，以順應乎其間。雖不悉中，亦思過半焉。視諸審樂知德者，不既有間矣乎？臣今也幸而蒙成於百執事，且將億之曰：庶幾其有名世者出是舉焉，俾臣幸復蒙成于將
translation_en:
…may come close to being obscured. Thus the ancients found it difficult to understand words and music. Have you already gained some insight into these things?

Your servant is untalented: how could I dare hope to equal the ancients? I can only reverently embody the sage Son of Heaven’s virtuous intention to honor refinement and restrain superficiality, extending it into practice. What matters is that writing clarify principles and serve practical purposes, without pursuing the abstruse and empty; that it comprehend what is appropriate in past and present, without flaunting vast learning to show off; and that it possess depth, substance, and cultivated elegance, without flattery or frivolous cleverness merely to attract eyes and ears. Taking what you say to gauge what you aspire to, I maintain a mind as empty as a mirror and as impartial as a balanced scale, responding accordingly among these writings. Though I may not judge everything correctly, I will have grasped more than half. Yet, compared with those who discern virtue through examining music, is there not still a considerable distance?

Your servant has now fortunately benefited from the accomplishments of all the officials concerned, and would venture this hope: perhaps someone who will win renown in his age will emerge from this examination, allowing your servant the good fortune of benefiting once again from another’s accomplishments in the time to…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
來如其無幸焉臣獨且柰之何
人亦有言實中其聲者謂之端
實不中其聲者謂之款款言不
用奸乃不生嗚呼懋戒哉孰知
聲實之不中其究為奸也哉惟
昔先臣嘗典文于兹蓋思延陵
之理樂而嘆東南之美也臣於
===
是重有感而述焉以告諸賢以
對揚
聖天子休命
奉訓大夫右春坊右諭德倫以訓
謹序
alt_text:
來如其無幸焉臣獨且奈之何
人亦有言實中其聲者謂之端
實不中其聲者謂之款款言不
用奸乃不生嗚呼懋戒哉孰知
聲實之不中其究爲奸也哉惟
昔先臣嘗典文于兹蓋思延陵
之理樂而嘆東南之美也臣於
是重有感而述焉以告諸賢以
===
對揚
聖天子休命
奉訓大夫右春坊右諭德倫錫
謹序
punctuated:
來。如其無幸焉，臣獨且柰之何？人亦有言：「實中其聲者謂之端，實不中其聲者謂之款。款言不用，奸乃不生。」嗚呼，懋戒哉！孰知聲實之不中，其究為奸也哉？惟昔先臣嘗典文于兹，蓋思延陵之理樂而嘆東南之美也。臣於是重有感而述焉，以告諸賢，以對揚聖天子休命。
奉訓大夫、右春坊右諭德倫以訓謹序。
translation_en:
…in the future. Should I not enjoy such good fortune, what then could I alone do about it? There is also a saying: “When substance accords with reputation, this is called uprightness; when substance does not accord with reputation, this is called deception. When deceptive words find no acceptance, wickedness does not arise.” Ah, take earnest warning! Who realizes that a failure of reputation to accord with substance ultimately leads to wickedness? Formerly, my late father presided over the literary examination here. Reflecting on the Lord of Yanling’s understanding of music, he marveled at the excellence of the southeast. These thoughts stir me once more, and I have written them down to inform you worthy gentlemen and to acknowledge and proclaim the august Son of Heaven’s gracious command.
Preface respectfully composed by Lun Yixun, Grand Master for Exemplary Instruction and Right Mentor in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent.

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
古之學者為己今之學者為人
故君子之道本諸身徵諸庶民考諸三王
而不繆建諸天地而不悖質諸鬼神而
無疑百世以俟聖人而不惑
五畝之宅樹牆下以桑匹婦蠶之則老者
足以衣帛矣五母雞二母彘無失其時
老者足以無失肉矣百畝之田匹夫耕
===
之八口之家可以無飢矣所謂西伯善
養老者制其田里教之樹畜導其妻子
使養其老五十非帛不煖七十非肉不
飽不煖不飽謂之凍餒文王之民無凍
餒之老者此之謂也
易
泰小往大來吉亨則是天地交而萬物通
也上下交而其志同也內陽而外陰內
健而外順內君子而外小人君子道長

足以衣帛矣五母雞二母彘無失其時
老者足以無失肉矣百畝之田匹夫耕
===
之八口之家可以無饑矣所謂西伯善
養老者制其田里教之樹畜導其妻子
使養其老五十非帛不煖七十非肉不
飽不煖不飽謂之凍餒文王之民無凍
餒之老者此之謂也
易
泰小往大來吉亨則是天地交而萬物通
也上下交而其志同也内陽而外陰内
健而外順内君子而外小人君子道長

第壹塲

四書

古之學者為己，今之學者為人。

故君子之道，本諸身，徵諸庶民，考諸三王而不繆，建諸天地而不悖，質諸鬼神而無疑，百世以俟聖人而不惑。

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Scholars of antiquity learned for their own sake; scholars today learn for the sake of others.”

“Thus the gentleman’s Way is rooted in his own person and verified among the common people. Tested against the Three Kings, it is without error; established before Heaven and Earth, it does not conflict with them; submitted to the spirits, it leaves no doubt. He can await a sage a hundred generations hence without misgiving.”

“On a homestead of five mu, plant mulberries beneath the walls. If one woman tends the silkworms, the elderly will have enough silk to wear. Keep five hens and two sows, and do not miss their breeding seasons: the elderly will have an uninterrupted supply of meat. If one man tills a hundred mu of fields, a household of eight mouths can be free from hunger. When it is said that the Lord of the West was skilled at caring for the elderly, this means that he regulated their fields and homesteads, taught them to plant trees and rear livestock, and guided their wives and children so that they could support their elderly. At fifty, one cannot keep warm without silk; at seventy, one cannot eat one’s fill without meat. To lack warmth and sufficient food is what is meant by suffering from cold and hunger. Among King Wen’s people, no elderly person suffered from cold or hunger. This is what the saying means.”

Book of Changes

“Tai (Peace): the small departs and the great arrives. Auspicious; success. This means that Heaven and Earth interact and all things communicate freely; those above and those below interact and share the same purpose. Yang is within and yin without; strength is within and compliance without; gentlemen are within and petty men without. The Way of the gentleman grows…”

translation_en:
…and the way of petty men wanes.

Nine in the second place: it is beneficial to remain correct, for one takes the mean as one’s aim.

The alternation of yin and yang is called the Way. What continues it is goodness; what brings it to completion is one’s nature. The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom. The common people use it daily without knowing it; thus the way of the gentleman is rarely understood.

Only after there are fathers and sons are there rulers and ministers.

Book of Documents

Be mindful! In leading undertakings and initiating affairs, be careful concerning your statutes. Be reverent! Repeatedly examine your accomplishments. Be reverent!

The sages have counsels and instructions, clearly attested, firmly established, and preserved. The former kings could heed Heaven’s warnings, and their ministers could maintain constant laws. The hundred officials diligently assisted their sovereign, making his discernment ever brighter.

Consider what is good before acting, and act only at the proper time.

Act with discernment, and there will be achievement; be generous and magnanimous, and there will be ample success.

Book of Odes

In the tenth month, crickets come beneath our beds. We stop up holes and smoke out rats, block the north-facing windows, and plaster the doors shut. Ah, my wife and children! The year is about to turn; enter this room and dwell here. In the sixth month we eat wild plums and wild grapes; in the seventh month we boil mallows and beans. In the eighth month we knock down jujubes; in the tenth month we harvest rice. With it we make spring wine, to bring the blessing of long life.

Record of Rites (Liji)
The Son of Heaven performs the spring yue sacrifice separately [?], and the summer di, autumn chang, and winter zheng sacrifices as combined ancestral sacrifices. When the feudal lords perform the yue sacrifice, they do not perform the di; when they perform the di, they do not perform the chang; when they perform the chang, they do not perform the zheng; when they perform the zheng, they do not perform the yue. The feudal lords perform the yue separately [?]; for the di, they alternate between a separate sacrifice [?] and a combined sacrifice; the chang and zheng are combined sacrifices.
At midday he comes again and does likewise; at evening he comes again and does likewise.
His words are concise yet clear, subtle yet excellent; he uses few comparisons yet makes himself understood. He may be said to enable others to carry on his purpose.
The people regard their ruler as their heart; the ruler regards the people as his body.

先軫郤克趙衰宋之華元楚之子文蔿
賈秦之百里奚鄭之子産吳之季札之
數子者皆能尊社稷庇人民傑然一代
也然攷其事功大者僅能輔其主以主
夏盟餘皆保全境土而已或者乃謂春
秋陰陽氣運之厄有以成吾道之厄雖

translation_en:
…our Sagely Founder took sixteen years. Why was there such a difference in the speed with which success was achieved? As for succeeding to the throne, why did the emperor undertake three expeditions in his imperial chariot to suppress the powerful northern Hu, following Emperor Wu’s territorial strategy rather than Emperors Wen and Jing’s policy of allowing the people respite? In the gengzi year of Yongle [1420], the capital was established in the north, yet during the Hongxi and Xuande reigns the designations “temporary imperial residence” and “Nanjing” underwent successive changes. Whose achievement was it, then, that ultimately established the foundation for ten thousand generations, enduring to this day? Please set out your answers point by point in your essay. The Book of Odes says: “Unfold these thoughts and ponder them; we go forth seeking only stability.”
Question: The flourishing and decline of talented men are bound up with the cycles of cosmic vital energy. We have no leisure here to discuss the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun or the Three Dynasties. Over the roughly two hundred years of the Spring and Autumn period, although the integrity of the primordial vital energy was dispersed as the realm’s mountains and rivers were divided, talented men never ceased to arise. Such men as Bao Shu and Guan Zhong of Qi; Jiu Fan, Xian Zhen, Xi Ke, and Zhao Cui of Jin; Hua Yuan of Song; Ziwen and Wei Jia of Chu; Baili Xi of Qin; Zichan of Zheng; and Ji Zha of Wu were all able to uphold their states and protect their people, standing out as eminent men of their age. Yet when we examine their achievements, even the greatest could do no more than help their rulers preside over the covenants of the Chinese states; the others merely preserved their territories intact. title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
偉人特起其才亦無所施然歟否歟漢
唐全盛之際其氣運昌矣而人才之名
者曰蕭曹丙魏曰房杜姚宋不知諸人
當時所建立者視春秋數子高下何如
耶又不知春秋數子復生其時其功烈
所就當何如耶或者乃謂春秋數子非
漢唐諸人所及當歟否歟孔子曰如有
用我吾其爲東周孟子曰以齊王猶反
手又不拘拘於氣運何歟諸葛亮志决
===
身殲不能一鼎分之勢狄仁傑秉彛向
晦乃能成取日之功其成敗不同豈亦
氣運爲之歟願究極根柢之論毋徒騁
浮詞侈然曰博洽
問三代之後帝王之治不復見矣世儒每
致意焉董仲舒以漢武帝王心未加也
對策曰設誠於內而致行之則三王何

translation_en:
…even when extraordinary men arose, their talents had no scope for employment. Is this so, or not? At the height of the Han and Tang dynasties, their cosmic fortunes flourished. Among their renowned men of talent were Xiao He, Cao Shen, Bing Ji, and Wei Xiang, and Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, Yao Chong, and Song Jing. How did these men’s accomplishments in their own times compare with those of the aforementioned men of the Spring and Autumn period? And had those men of the Spring and Autumn period been born again in those times, what achievements might they have attained? Some maintain that the men of the Han and Tang could not match those of the Spring and Autumn period. Is this judgment correct, or not? Confucius said, “If someone were to employ me, might I not establish a Zhou in the east?” Mencius said, “To attain true kingship through Qi would be as easy as turning over one’s hand.” Why, then, were they not constrained by considerations of cosmic fortune? Zhuge Liang remained resolute until his death, yet could not unify the realm divided among three powers like the legs of a tripod. Di Renjie upheld the enduring moral principles amid gathering darkness, yet succeeded in recovering the sun—that is, restoring the Tang. Were their differing outcomes of success and failure also brought about by cosmic fortune? Please pursue the argument to its very roots; do not merely parade empty words and boast of your extensive learning.

Question: Since the Three Dynasties, the government of the ancient emperors and kings has not been seen again. Confucian scholars through the ages have repeatedly given this matter their attention. Dong Zhongshu considered that Emperor Wu of Han had not yet applied the mind of a true king. In his response to a policy question, he said, “If you establish sincerity within and carry it fully into practice, how would you differ from the Three Kings?” Wang Ji urged Emperor Xuan to consider establishing a lasting policy for ten thousand generations and to raise his enlightened sovereign to the flourishing heights of the Three Dynasties. title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
行王道期致治如三代之隆而後已邵
子論皇極經世曰苟有命世之人興焉
則雖民如夷狄三變而帝道可舉信斯
言也行王道者何先建長策者何術帝
道若為而舉王心若為而加其言皆可
底績而時弗之庸耶抑否也方今
聖明在上志復隆古興道致治千載一時子諸
子其酌先民之論商帝王之畧以佐下
風於萬一不亦可乎
===
問周禮以鄉三物教萬民而賓興之而後
世取士惟以經義夫經義特三物之一
爾豈亦可兼其二歟王制執左道亂民
者有禁而今之老佛亦左道也何蔓延
而不能去歟六經之道甚明而易行窮
經者乃支離於章句文詞之末而不復
究心聖賢之旨豈詞章亦可謂道歟學
春秋者知正朝廷以正百官之理而以
經術為帝師何不能止外戚之强長易

問：《周禮》以鄉三物教萬民，而賓興之，而後世取士惟以經義。夫經義特三物之一爾，豈亦可兼其二歟？《王制》執左道亂民者有禁，而今之老佛亦左道也，何蔓延而不能去歟？六經之道甚明而易行，窮經者乃支離於章句文詞之末，而不復究心聖賢之旨，豈詞章亦可謂道歟？學《春秋》者知正朝廷以正百官之理，而以經術為帝師，何不能止外戚之强長？《易》
translation_en:
…to practice the Kingly Way, resolved not to rest until government attained the flourishing condition of the Three Dynasties. Master Shao, discussing Supreme Principles for Ordering the World (Huangji jingshi), said: “If a person destined to lead an age should arise, then even if the people were like the Yi and Di, through three transformations the Way of the Emperors could be put into practice.” If these words are true, what should come first in practicing the Kingly Way? By what means should a lasting policy be established? How can the Way of the Emperors be put into practice, and how can a kingly heart be applied? Could all these proposals have produced results, but their times failed to employ them? Or was this not so? Today our sagacious sovereign reigns above, intent on restoring the flourishing age of antiquity. This is an opportunity encountered once in a thousand years to promote the Way and achieve good government. Would it not be fitting for you gentlemen to weigh the arguments of earlier worthies and deliberate upon the strategies of emperors and kings, thereby contributing even the slightest assistance to those serving below?

Question: The Rites of Zhou teaches the myriad people through the three subjects of district instruction and then honors worthy men as guests and recommends them for office. Yet later generations select officials solely through interpretation of the classics. Interpretation of the classics is only one of those three subjects; can it also encompass the other two? The “Royal Regulations” prohibits adhering to heterodox ways that disorder the people. The teachings of Laozi and the Buddha today are likewise heterodox ways: why do they spread unchecked and prove impossible to eliminate? The Way of the Six Classics is exceedingly clear and easy to practice, yet those who study the classics exhaustively become lost in fragmented attention to the incidental details of chapters, sentences, and literary expression, and no longer devote themselves to investigating the meaning intended by the sages and worthies. Can literary composition itself be called the Way? One who studied the Spring and Autumn Annals understood the principle of rectifying the court in order to rectify the hundred officials; yet, though he became the emperor’s teacher through his classical learning, why could he not halt the growing power of imperial in-laws? translation_en:
…scholars of the Changes know how to discuss the methods by which emperors and kings raised worthy men to office; yet when an eminent Confucian scholar occupied the position of chief minister, why could he not secure the rightful position of the Prince of Qinghe? Could it be that classical learning cannot be fully put into practice? The writings of Buddhism and Daoism delude the world and deceive the people. Earlier Confucian scholars repudiated them with great severity and vigor; why, then, are they still transmitted alongside the Six Classics? Those who study the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi can bring about tranquil government; yet why did the ruler who styled himself “Lord of the Dao” bring on the calamity of the Jingkang era? Those who understand Chan Buddhism can comprehend the boundary between life and death; yet why did the ruler who offered his own person in service to the Buddha fail to avert the peril at Taicheng? Could these teachings contain something useful, while people differ in applying them well or badly? We now wish those who embrace the meaning of the Classics also to possess virtuous conduct, with their abilities embodying the reality of both substance and practical application [?]; we wish all who practice heterodox arts to recognize that these must be prohibited and eradicated, so that the world is free of the error of revering and trusting them. By what means can this actually be accomplished? Explain in detail, so that we may discern the direction of your aspirations.

text:
足言矣其又信然耶或欲先懲奸商之
罔利或欲先恤竈戶之流亡或謂邉儲
不納本色則鹽法終無補是三說者孰
急或言屯軍病民可罷或言清查擾民
可已或謂不如姑緩其舊而增置其新
是三說者孰近諸君子究心斯世奚啻
熟講此耶願聞之具以質言

translation_en: …worth mentioning. Is this, in turn, really so? Some wish first to punish unscrupulous merchants for their fraudulent pursuit of profit; others wish first to relieve the plight of salt-producing households that have fled their homes; still others maintain that unless frontier granaries receive supplies in kind, the salt administration will ultimately be of no benefit. Which of these three proposals is most urgent? Some say that military agricultural colonists burden the people and that the system may be abolished; others say that investigations and audits harass the people and may be discontinued; still others maintain that it would be better for the time being to relax enforcement concerning existing military agricultural colonies and establish additional new ones. Which of these three proposals is most sound? You gentlemen devote your minds to the affairs of this age: surely you have done more than merely discuss these matters thoroughly? I wish to hear your views; set them out fully in plain words.

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
古之學者爲己今之學者爲人
王之省
同考試官訓導王批此題作者類不責
心顧以世變爲諉惟此篇辭嚴義精發出聖人
警教深旨豈亦爲爲己之學者與
同考試官教諭楊批古今學者爲己爲
人之分决於用心得失之際說得親切令人省

First Session

Four Books

“The scholars of antiquity learned for themselves; the scholars of today learn for others.”

Wang Zhixing

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Assistant Instructor: Most who write on this topic fail to hold the mind accountable, instead making changes in the times their excuse. This essay alone, with its rigorous language and precise interpretation, brings out the profound intent of the Sage’s warning and instruction. Might its author also be one who pursues learning for himself?

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: The distinction between ancient and present-day scholars—learning for oneself or for others—is determined by whether they direct their minds rightly or wrongly. No essay surpasses this one in explaining the matter pertinently and making readers reflect and take heed. For this reason it has been selected for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Left Assistant Adviser (左贊善): Its words are sincere and incisive, well worth reading.

Comment by Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher (右諭德): This is writing of consequence.

The Sage speaks of scholars ancient and modern: in establishing their intentions, they differ in turning inward or outward. Learning begins with establishing one’s intentions. The distinction between learning for oneself and learning for others is what underlies the distinction between ancient and modern scholars. Can scholars fail to know what they must examine carefully? Profound indeed is the Sage’s concern for the world!

Now, among the affairs of the world, there are certainly those that arise from the subtle beginnings of a single thought yet go astray by a thousand miles. translation_en:
…and acquired extensive knowledge of past deeds. They certainly pursued learning with reverence, humility, and timely diligence. Yet they broadened their literary learning to attain the Way, refined their language to establish sincerity, and acquainted themselves widely with the words and deeds of the past to nurture virtue. In their thoughts there was never any intention of carelessly deceiving themselves. Why was this? Because what their hearts pursued lay within. They reasoned: “If I fail to fulfill what is inherently mine by nature or what I ought to do by virtue of my duties, then the human Way is deficient.” Thus they worked diligently, finding each day too short, and exerted themselves to the utmost in every means of seeking this fulfillment. Proceeding along this course, they ultimately fully realized the natures of people and things, joining with Heaven and Earth and assisting their transforming and nourishing work. This was simply to establish others as they established themselves, and to help others attain fulfillment as they attained it themselves. What could there be beyond this?

People today are otherwise. Their literary learning is hardly narrow, their language hardly unpolished, and their knowledge of past words and deeds hardly scant. They too have pursued learning, chanting texts and poring over their books. Yet they broaden their literary learning to amuse themselves with external things, polish their language to embellish falsehood, and acquire extensive knowledge of past words and deeds to boast of its abundance and vie in ornate display. In their thoughts there is never the substance of quietly finding satisfaction within themselves. Why is this? Because what their hearts pursue lies outside. They reason: “I excel at this—that is enough; I am capable of this—that is enough.” If they possess even a little knowledge [?], they fear that others will not know they possess it. Thus they too work diligently and find each day too short; they will go to any lengths to alter themselves to please others. Proceeding along this course, they ultimately violate the Way to seek the praise of the common people, and oppose the common people to satisfy their own desires. This too …

故君子之道，本諸身，徵諸庶民，考諸三王而不繆，建諸天地而不悖，質諸鬼神而無疑，百世以俟聖人而不惑。

translation_en:
…merely calculating achievements and seeking profit, deceiving the world and stealing a reputation. How could they have gained anything? Thus those who learn for their own sake ultimately bring other things to fulfillment; those who learn for others’ approval ultimately lose themselves. Given this, learners who fail to recognize what requires careful discrimination are profoundly deluded indeed! Alas! This is the distinction between righteousness and profit, sincerity and falsity; upon it depend the flourishing or decline of the moral order and the good government or disorder of the state. Later, Zisi developed the disposition expressed in “wearing brocade beneath a plain gauze robe,” carrying it to its ultimate culmination in bringing peace to all under Heaven through profound reverence. Mengzi spoke of the evils of loving profit, which culminate in the grave wrong of abandoning one’s parents and forgetting one’s ruler. Between applying the mind rightly and wrongly, the resulting benefits and harms lie more than a thousand miles apart. How fearsome this is! This is why the sage showed such earnest concern for all under Heaven and for later generations.
Therefore the Way of the gentleman is rooted in his own person, verified among the common people, tested against the Three Kings without error, established before Heaven and Earth without contradiction, submitted to ghosts and spirits without doubt, and awaits a sage a hundred generations hence without uncertainty.
Wang Hui
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: Those who write on this topic are either stale or muddled. This essay alone is pure and correct in both expression and reasoning; reading it inspires awe and respect.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yan, Instructor: Those who write on this topic generally discuss the individual and the people as counterparts, badly misjudging their relative importance. This essay alone places the emphasis on the individual himself. Moreover, its language is not superficial, and its reasoning comes through clearly of itself. It may serve as a model.

固其屈伸之機也質之奚疑哉後聖者生乎百
世之下若遠而難知也然其所以建立於異世
===
者則不能違理以自法焉君子斟酌之權固其
推行之準也俟之奚惑哉吁一德立而制作之
達於無間如此然則君子之身其萬化之原而
王道之紀者歟抑攷程子之言曰有天德便可
語王道其要只在謹獨夫獨者存於一念之微
而天地萬物舉不能違焉者性命之同也而其
始則由於學故不知學而能知性命之理者鮮
矣故不知性命之理而能謹獨者鮮矣不能謹
獨而可與語王道者未之有也後世徒以私意
punctuated: 在周者猶夫在殷也，其在殷者猶夫在夏也。考之，則先後一揆矣，夫何繆？大而天地，其覆載生成之功雖則異形，而理之所同則有不可得而違者。其確然者，其易也；其隤然者，其簡也。以建之，則上下同流矣，夫何悖？至若鬼神者，用妙乎萬物之內，若幽而不測也。然其所以運行於造化者，則不能外理以自神焉。君子通變之宜，固其屈伸之機也，質之奚疑哉？後聖者生乎百世之下，若遠而難知也。然其所以建立於異世者，則不能違理以自法焉。君子斟酌之權，固其推行之準也，俟之奚惑哉？吁！一德立而制作之達於無間如此，然則君子之身，其萬化之原而王道之紀者歟？抑攷程子之言曰：「有天德便可語王道，其要只在謹獨。」夫獨者，存於一念之微，而天地萬物舉不能違焉者，性命之同也。而其始則由於學，故不知學而能知性命之理者鮮矣。故不知性命之理而能謹獨者鮮矣。不能謹獨而可與語王道者，未之有也。後世徒以私意
translation_en:
…what prevailed in Zhou was like what prevailed in Yin, and what prevailed in Yin was like what prevailed in Xia. Examining these, one finds a single standard throughout earlier and later times: what discrepancy could there be? Vast as Heaven and Earth are, although their achievements in covering and supporting, generating and completing things take different forms, they share a principle from which neither can depart. Heaven’s firmness is its ease; Earth’s yielding receptivity is its simplicity. Establishing institutions by this principle, one joins the common flow above and below: what contradiction could there be? As for ghosts and spirits, their workings are wondrous within the myriad things, seemingly hidden and unfathomable. Yet in their operation within the processes of creation and transformation, they cannot stand outside principle and exercise spiritual efficacy on their own. The gentleman’s fitting responses to change are precisely the workings of their contraction and expansion. What doubt could there be in testing his actions against them? Sages to come, born a hundred generations hence, seem remote and difficult to know. Yet in what they establish in another age, they cannot depart from principle and make rules of their own. The gentleman’s discretionary judgment is precisely the standard by which they will put their measures into practice. What uncertainty could there be in awaiting them?

Ah! Once this single virtue is established, the institutions fashioned through it extend everywhere without obstruction. Is not the gentleman’s own person, then, the source of the myriad transformations and the governing thread of the kingly Way? Consider, moreover, Master Cheng’s words: “Possessing Heaven’s virtue, one may then speak of the kingly Way. The essential point lies solely in vigilance when alone.” This aloneness resides in the subtle inception of a single thought; that Heaven, Earth, and all things alike cannot depart from it is owing to the principle they share in their nature and Heaven-conferred endowment. Yet the beginning lies in learning. Thus, few who do not understand learning can understand the principle of nature and Heaven-conferred endowment. Likewise, few who do not understand that principle can be vigilant when alone. There has never been anyone incapable of such vigilance with whom one could discuss the kingly Way. Those of later ages, relying merely on private intentions…

小智紛更於天下自謂足以通時之變而不知
其擾天下也已甚矣嗚呼以此爲訓猶有變法

五畝之宅樹牆下以桑匹婦蠶之則老者
足以衣帛矣五母雞二母彘無失其時
老者足以無失肉矣百畝之田匹夫耕
之八口之家可以無饑矣所謂西伯善
養老者制其田里教之樹畜導其妻子
使養其老五十非帛不煖七十非肉不

餒之老者此之謂也

小智紛更於天下，自謂足以通時之變，而不知其擾天下也已甚矣。嗚呼！以此爲訓，猶有變法賈禍如宋煕豐之所爲者，悲夫！

五畝之宅，樹牆下以桑，匹婦蠶之，則老者足以衣帛矣。五母雞，二母彘，無失其時，老者足以無失肉矣。百畝之田，匹夫耕之，八口之家可以無饑矣。所謂西伯善養老者，制其田里，教之樹畜，導其妻子，使養其老。五十非帛不煖，七十非肉不飽。不煖不飽，謂之凍餒。文王之民無凍餒之老者，此之謂也。

鄭維誠

同考試官教諭劉批：周文善養老意，體貼得出。

同考試官教授高批：王道養民善處，不過因其自然之利而已。是作得旨，用錄。

考試官左贊善張批：詞約而理明。

考試官右諭德倫批：勁徹。
translation_en:
…with petty cleverness, they make a welter of changes throughout the realm, claiming that these suffice to meet changing circumstances, unaware that they have already disturbed the realm excessively. Alas! Even with this as a warning, there were still those who changed the laws and brought calamity upon themselves, as in the Xining and Yuanfeng eras of the Song. How lamentable!

On a homestead of five mu, plant mulberry trees beneath the walls and let one woman rear silkworms: the elderly will then have enough silk to wear. Keep five hens and two sows, without missing their breeding seasons, and the elderly will have enough to go without lacking meat [?]. Let one man cultivate a hundred mu of fields, and a household of eight mouths can be free from hunger. What is meant by saying that the Lord of the West excelled at caring for the elderly is that he regulated their fields and homesteads, taught them to plant trees and raise livestock, and guided their wives and children so that they could support their elderly. At fifty, one cannot keep warm without silk; at seventy, one cannot feel full without meat. To lack warmth and sufficient food is called suffering from cold and hunger. This is what is meant by saying that among King Wen’s people there were no elderly persons suffering from cold and hunger.

Zheng Weicheng.

Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor of the County Confucian School, comments: “The meaning of King Wen of Zhou’s excellence in caring for the elderly is sensitively brought out.”

Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor of the Prefectural Confucian School, comments: “The excellence of the Kingly Way in nourishing the people consists simply in making use of the benefits naturally available to them. This composition captures the essential meaning; selected for inclusion.”

Examiner Zhang, Left Mentor, comments: “The language is concise and the reasoning clear.”

Examiner Lun, Right Adviser, comments: “Forceful and penetrating.”

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
大賢詳聖人養老之政言其爲因民之利而利
之也夫王人者將以導利而布之上下者也而
文王之所以利乎民者皆因之民焉此其爲善
養老歟孟子之意若曰王道之行必始諸仁政
而仁政之施莫善於文王吾嘗攷而知其政矣
彼患夫老者之不足於衣食也於是乎有樹畜
之教焉五畝之宅樹墻下以桑而匹婦蠶之則
杼軸有餘帛五十者可以衣之以卒歲矣五母
雞二母彘而以時育之則孕字有常候七十者
===
可以不至於徒食矣彼患夫黎民之累於俯仰
也於是乎有常産之制焉授一夫以百畝之田
而使之盡耕斂之力則穀不可勝食而八口之
家不至於有饑矣文王之政如此然而天下之
人自北海而來焉自東海而來焉莫不曰是善
養老者夫所謂善者豈有他哉亦惟因其田里
而制之因其樹畜而教之因其妻子而導之使
自相爲養爾矣豈必家賜而人益之耶五十必
帛而後煖七十必肉而後飽不煖不飽於是有

translation_en:
The great worthy elaborates upon the sage’s policies for supporting the aged, explaining that he benefited the people by building upon the resources already available to them. One who rules the people [?] should guide the sources of benefit and distribute them among those above and below. Yet all the means by which King Wen benefited the people drew upon the people themselves. Was this not what made him so good at supporting the aged?

Mencius’s meaning might be expressed thus: “The practice of the kingly Way must begin with benevolent government, and in administering benevolent government none surpassed King Wen. I have examined his policies and come to understand them. He worried that the aged lacked adequate clothing and food, and therefore provided instruction in planting and raising livestock. On a homestead of five mu, mulberries were planted beneath the walls, and a woman tended silkworms. The loom would then yield silk cloth to spare, and those aged fifty could wear it throughout the year. Five hens and two sows were raised according to the proper seasons, so that breeding and the rearing of their young followed a regular schedule, and those aged seventy would not have to eat their meals without meat.

“He worried that the common people were burdened by supporting their parents above and their children below, and therefore established a system of secure livelihoods. Each man was allotted a hundred mu of land and enabled to devote his full effort to cultivation and harvesting. There would then be more grain than could be eaten, and a household of eight would not go hungry. Such were King Wen’s policies. People throughout the realm came to him from the northern sea and from the eastern sea, all saying that he was one who excelled at supporting the aged.

“What else could this so-called excellence consist in? He simply established arrangements based on their fields and homesteads, instructed them in accordance with their planting and animal husbandry, and guided them through their wives and children, enabling them to support one another. Why should it have been necessary to bestow gifts upon every household and give additional aid to every individual? At fifty, people need silk to be warm; at seventy, they need meat to be fully nourished. Without warmth and adequate nourishment, there are then …

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
不得其養而凍餒者矣文王之民亦惟以其所
制者而養之以其所教者而養之以其所導者
而養之斯無凍餒之老爾矣曷嘗利之以為庸
耶夫利不外於民而愛則周民皆被其澤而惠
不費其曰善養老者非此之謂歟向使文王求
一國之老而人為之所焉則其為惠也亦淺矣
是豈聖人之所謂政哉雖然文王何以得此耶
書曰克明德蓋明德則仁仁而後能愛人明德
則公公而後能處物此絜矩之道而平天下之
===
本也不然則田齊之惠可以言仁而管仲之知
比迹湯武矣而何功烈如彼其卑耶故觀□於孟
子之論則王霸之辨昭矣
易
泰小往大來吉亨則是天地交而萬物通
也上下交而其志同也內陽而外陰內
健而外順內君子而外小人君子道長
小人道消也

punctuated:
不得其養而凍餒者矣。文王之民，亦惟以其所制者而養之，以其所教者而養之，以其所導者而養之，斯無凍餒之老爾矣。曷嘗利之以為庸耶？夫利不外於民而愛則周，民皆被其澤而惠不費，其曰善養老者，非此之謂歟？向使文王求一國之老而人為之所焉，則其為惠也亦淺矣。是豈聖人之所謂政哉？雖然，文王何以得此耶？《書》曰：「克明德。」蓋明德則仁，仁而後能愛人；明德則公，公而後能處物。此絜矩之道而平天下之本也。不然，則田齊之惠可以言仁，而管仲之知比迹湯武矣，而何功烈如彼其卑耶？故觀□於孟子之論，則王霸之辨昭矣。

易

泰，小往大來，吉亨。則是天地交而萬物通也，上下交而其志同也。內陽而外陰，內健而外順，內君子而外小人，君子道長，小人道消也。
translation_en:
…there will be those who lack proper sustenance and suffer cold and hunger. Among King Wen’s people, they merely supported the aged through the arrangements he had instituted, the practices he had taught, and the guidance he had provided; thus there were no elderly people suffering cold or hunger. When did he ever claim the benefits he bestowed upon them as his own achievement? The resources for their benefit came entirely from the people, yet his care reached everyone. All the people received his bounty, yet his beneficence entailed no expense. Is this not what is meant by saying that he was good at caring for the aged? Had King Wen instead sought out all the aged in his realm and personally provided a place for each, his beneficence would have been shallow indeed. Could this be what the sages called government? Yet how did King Wen attain this? The Book of Documents says: “He was able to make virtue manifest.” Making virtue manifest brings benevolence, and only through benevolence can one care for others; making virtue manifest brings impartiality, and only through impartiality can one deal properly with things. This is the Way of the measuring square—the principle of reciprocity—and the foundation for bringing peace to all under Heaven. Otherwise, the beneficence of the Tian house of Qi could be called benevolence, and Guan Zhong’s wisdom could rank alongside the deeds of Tang and Wu. Why, then, were their achievements so inferior? Thus, examining [illegible character] in light of Mengzi’s discussion [?], the distinction between true kingship and hegemony becomes clear.

Book of Changes

Tai (Peace): The small departs and the great comes; auspicious and successful. This means that Heaven and Earth interact, and all things communicate freely; those above and those below interact, and their purposes are shared. Within is yang, and without is yin; within is strength, and without is compliance; within are gentlemen, and without are petty men. The way of gentlemen grows, and the way of petty men wanes.

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導王批通篇圓粹明確無
一常語愛君憂國之意尤溢於言外保泰之功
愚端有望於子矣
同考試官教諭楊批世道之泰本於君
臣之志同而其所以同者係於理欲邪正之分
塲中士子知此者絕少子能言之可以薦矣
考試官左贊善張批是知致泰之理者結
更有味
考試官右諭德倫批發揮融暢
===
聖人傳泰之彖而推言乎世道之所由泰也夫
泰不生於泰而必有所由致也聖人傳泰之彖
而推言之無餘蘊矣伏羲畫卦而名之曰泰以
乾下而坤上也文王繫辭而曰小往大來吉亨
以卦體卦變而要其占也夫子釋之以謂啓泰
之運者存乎天而成泰之治者存乎人夫乾天
道也君道也夫坤地道也臣道也乾下坤上則
是天地相感而泰和之氣充塞化機流通而萬
物之性咸若非復屯難之時也君不苦於臣之

Fuxi drew the hexagram and named it Tai because Qian (Heaven) is below and Kun (Earth) above. King Wen appended the words, “The small departs and the great arrives: auspicious and successful,” drawing upon the hexagram’s structure and transformations to summarize its divinatory meaning. …ten ministers.” They shared one heart and one virtue: this was concord. Chief Minister Wei Xiang’s thoroughly satisfying his sovereign’s wishes, and Jiefu’s holding his sovereign to the kingly Way, were also forms of concord. Why, then, were the results of their governance so far apart? Because of the difference between public-mindedness and private interest. Thus those united through the Way invariably flourish; those united through desire invariably bring disorder. Accordingly, sovereigns who wish to bring good government to the world and ministers who wish to serve their sovereign need only take care over what unites them.

“Yin and yang in alternation [?] are called the Way. What continues it is goodness; what brings it to completion is human nature. The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom. The common people use it daily without knowing it. Thus the Way of the gentleman is rarely understood.”

Yan Kezhong

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Assistant Instructor: The Way is not easy to discuss. Yet you have elucidated the purport of the sage’s discussion of the Way and, with particular earnestness, guided people toward the essentials of embodying it. Can this be called mere exposition of textual phrases? Having found you, I have genuine cause to congratulate myself.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: The Way of the gentleman is precisely the Way of alternating yin and yang. We can see that the great source of the Way comes from Heaven and that human beings cannot be without it. People possess it but simply fail to perceive it themselves. Examiner Lun, Right Mentor, comments: “The words of one who has insight are naturally distinctive.”

In speaking of the substance of the Way, the Great Commentary necessarily traces its original wholeness and makes clear how partiality arises. For the Way does not extend beyond yin and yang: this can be seen in their presence in Heaven and humankind. Had the sage himself not pointed it out and spoken of it, the Way would have remained all but hidden. Where, then, does the name ‘the Way’ originate? It is named for the alternation of yin and yang. The Way is the Supreme Ultimate: this speaks of the subtlety of its inherent condition. Yin and yang are activity and stillness: this speaks of the workings through which it operates. Those immersed in nothingness certainly cannot speak of the Way; but how could those confined to one aspect possess the Way in its entirety? Only when yin and yang unite their powers—yang active and yin still, each serving as the root of the other—do we have the inherent condition of the Supreme Ultimate and the whole substance of the Way. This is what is called the Way.

As this Way has its source in Heaven, its profound and august mandate flows without cease; its reality, free of falsity, is utterly sincere and undivided. It is pure and refined, without the slightest admixture: do we not call this goodness? As it is embodied in human beings, the Way of Qian brings about change and transformation, and each thing possesses its own principle. These principles are not borrowed from one another, and their greater and lesser measures are fixed. Each is integrally complete, without the slightest deficiency: do we not call this nature?

Although nature and Heaven’s mandate are the same, endowments of vital energy may differ. Thus some receive a partial endowment of vital energy and become benevolent. The benevolent go too far in action and no longer regard the Way as worth knowing. Others receive a partial endowment of vital energy and become knowing. The knowing go too far in knowledge and no longer regard the Way as worth practicing. As for the common people, they are uncomprehending, acting yet …

念哉！率作興事，慎乃憲。欽哉！屢省乃成。欽哉！
鄭維誠
同考試官教諭劉批：得皐陶作歌本旨，宜錄。
translation_en:
…without understanding, and practice without examining: though encompassed within this Way, they fall short in knowing and acting. Human nature is established within vital force; when constrained by vital force, it becomes one-sided. The Way resides in physical form; when confined to physical form, it becomes obscured. Thus, are not those who follow the Way of the noble person throughout their lives yet can comprehend it in its entirety very few? Yin and yang united as one constitute its fundamental substance; the particular predominance of either yin or yang constitutes one's endowment of vital force. If the noble person understands the source of this partiality and can comprehend the whole, the Way is not far away.
It has been said: the unity of activity and stillness lies in the Way; the unity of benevolence and wisdom lies in sagehood; and the unity of human nature and Heaven's Way lies in sincerity. The realm of sagehood and sincerity is not easily attained, yet the Way need not be sought outside oneself. Those who learn well need only turn back and seek it within their own hearts. For the heart is where the Way is fully present. Thus, by fully realizing one's heart, one knows one's nature and thereby knows Heaven; by preserving one's heart and nurturing one's nature, one establishes one's own destiny. How could the Way of sagehood and sincerity lie outside this? Hence there are few who, without understanding the heart, can be engaged in discussion of the Way.
Book of Documents
“Take heed! In leading undertakings and initiating affairs, be careful concerning your statutes. Be reverent! Repeatedly examine your accomplishments. Be reverent!”
Zheng Weicheng
Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: “This captures the original intent of Gao Yao in composing his song. It merits inclusion.”

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
敬乎哉莫匪君事也百工之熈臣之責也而所
以考厥成者將不在於君乎必也日以省月以
試而勤惰得有所稽言以考事以詢而廢置得
有所詔底可績者無以蔽其善奏罔功者無以
售其欺是盖因夫分職之已定者而程督勸課
之于以善始善終初非操切之爲也夫功之弗
覈或至於害成覈之弗審或至於滋僞於此處
之而可以無敬乎哉是則保盈成之治固在於
敕天而竭股肱之力尤資於元首皐陶責難之
===
意既發端於此矣抑考舜之初政載在典謨不
無事矣皐陶勸之率作而遽以慎憲繼之勸之
屢省而又終之以叢脞之戒然則孔子稱舜無
爲而治非耶盖握其機於上而久其道於天下
在勿忘勿助之間者也勿忘勿助之間者允執
厥中也是君道之恒也
聖有謨訓明徴定保先王克謹天戒臣人
克有常憲百官修輔厥后惟明明
李末

===

屢省而又終之以叢脞之戒然則孔子稱舜無

厥中也是君道之恒也
聖有謨訓明徵定保先王克謹天戒臣人
克有常憲百官修輔厥后惟明明
李末
punctuated:
敬乎哉？莫匪君事也。百工之熈，臣之責也，而所以考厥成者，將不在於君乎？必也日以省，月以試，而勤惰得有所稽；言以考，事以詢，而廢置得有所詔。底可績者，無以蔽其善；奏罔功者，無以售其欺。是盖因夫分職之已定者，而程督勸課之，于以善始善終，初非操切之爲也。夫功之弗覈，或至於害成；覈之弗審，或至於滋僞。於此處之，而可以無敬乎哉？是則保盈成之治，固在於敕天，而竭股肱之力，尤資於元首。皐陶責難之意，既發端於此矣。抑考舜之初政，載在典謨，不無事矣。皐陶勸之率作，而遽以慎憲繼之；勸之屢省，而又終之以叢脞之戒。然則孔子稱舜無爲而治，非耶？盖握其機於上，而久其道於天下，在勿忘勿助之間者也。勿忘勿助之間者，允執厥中也。是君道之恒也。
聖有謨訓，明徴定保。先王克謹天戒，臣人克有常憲，百官修輔，厥后惟明明。
李末
translation_en:
…without reverence? All these are the ruler’s affairs. Bringing the work of the many officials to fruition is the ministers’ responsibility, but does not assessing their accomplishments rest with the ruler? He must inspect them daily and test them monthly, so that diligence and indolence can be examined; assess their words and inquire into their deeds, so that instructions may be given concerning dismissal and appointment. Those who achieve results must not have their merits obscured; those who report achievements without accomplishing anything must not be allowed to pass off their deceit. This means taking the established division of duties as the basis for setting standards, supervising, encouraging, and evaluating officials, thereby ensuring a good beginning and a good end. It does not mean governing through harsh pressure. Failure to verify achievements may impair success; insufficient care in verification may foster deceit. In handling these matters, how could one dispense with reverence? Thus, preserving a government already flourishing and accomplished certainly depends on heeding Heaven; yet eliciting the full efforts of the ministers, its arms and legs, depends especially upon the ruler, its head. Gao Yao’s intention of demanding difficult things of his ruler is already apparent here.
Moreover, if we examine Shun’s early government as recorded in the Canons and Counsels, it was certainly not without activity. Gao Yao urged him to lead officials in their work, immediately following this with an exhortation to exercise care concerning established rules; he urged him to inspect them frequently, yet concluded with a warning against meddling in petty details. Was Confucius therefore wrong to praise Shun for governing through nonaction? Rather, holding the controlling mechanism from above and perpetuating his Way throughout the realm lie between neither neglecting it nor forcing its growth. To remain between neglect and forced growth is truly to hold fast to the mean. This is the constant principle of the ruler’s Way.
The sages have counsels and instructions: clearly verify them, establish them firmly, and preserve them. The former kings could heed Heaven’s warnings with care; their ministers could abide by constant rules. The hundred officials cultivated their duties and assisted their sovereign, and their sovereign was thereby enlightened indeed.
Li Mo.

思天戒之孔昭也審幾於一念之微而省括于
應政之際凡所以修德弭災者無所不用其極

Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: “The discussion clearly explains the idea of ruler and ministers cultivating themselves in concert.”
Associate Examiner Gao, Professor, comments: “Even before one finishes reading, it makes one alert. Surely it can serve to admonish!”
Examiner Zhang, Left Mentor, comments: “The phrasing is graceful and the meaning fully expressed.”
Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher, comments: “Clear and incisive.”
The sage kings’ teaching on preserving the state achieves its purpose only through the mutual cultivation of those above and below. Such mutual cultivation is the means of reaching Heaven, and therein lies the way to preserve the state. Could the sage kings’ teaching deceive us? This was the intent of the Marquis of Yin’s address to his troops when, at the king’s command, he marched against Xi and He.
What is valued in a ruler is that he makes Heaven’s heart his own; what is valued in a minister is that he makes the ruler’s heart his own. The counsels and teachings of our ancient sage kings remain. Their great plans originated in a single heart, and their lessons and warnings shine down through ten thousand generations. Their words disclose the crucial workings of rise and decline, which actual events can verify; their Way provides sound plans for establishing order, by which the state can be preserved. How is this teaching to be explained? The ruler’s duty is to assess affairs by the Way: he need only measure them against Heaven. If he pays no heed to Heaven’s warnings, he will indulge his feelings and give free rein to his desires, losing Heaven’s favor above. To what extremes might he not go? Thus the former kings did not attribute calamities and anomalies to fate; they invariably reflected on the utter clarity of Heaven’s warnings. They scrutinized the first stirrings within the subtle beginnings of a single thought and examined matters comprehensively [?] when attending to government. They exerted themselves to the utmost in every means of cultivating virtue and averting calamity. …

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
應厥職法守守夫常憲而已矣常憲之弗存則
將招權擅政上干天和何所不至哉故人臣不
以災變委之國必思天職之弗恭也恪遵乎憲
度之常而率由乎典章之舊凡所以奉公守法
者無敢有越厥志焉然人臣豈徒守常之爲貴
哉其必振師師之風以匡其君之不逮躬蹇蹇
之節以效其職之當爲補察之益盡于臣鄰修
省之誠協于上下夫然後爲之君者內無失德
而聽斷益精外無失政而照臨益廣兼天下之
===
視聽以作哲作謀憲皇天之聰明以克明克類
信乎爲明明后可以囘天眷而定邦家矣夫以
聖王之畏天若此其至而著之謨訓者若此其
嚴羲和之玩天戒而侮聖言尚何以容於斯世
哉抑愚觀羲和之職蓋唐虞命官之世而顓頊
氏重黎之遺也啓征有扈亦以威侮五行怠棄
三正言之古人重天事尚矣後是羲和無聞周
爲馮相保章列於天官之屬漢以太史兼掌天
官事守益微豈胤征之後則遂削其世而貶其

視聽以作哲作謀憲皇天之聰明以克明克類
信乎爲明明后可以回天眷而奠邦家矣夫以
聖王之畏天若此其至而著之謨訓者若此其

官事守益微豈胤征之後則遂斷其世而終其
punctuated:
應厥職，法守，守夫常憲而已矣。常憲之弗存，則將招權擅政，上干天和，何所不至哉？故人臣不以災變委之國，必思天職之弗恭也。恪遵乎憲度之常，而率由乎典章之舊，凡所以奉公守法者，無敢有越厥志焉。然人臣豈徒守常之爲貴哉？其必振師師之風，以匡其君之不逮；躬蹇蹇之節，以效其職之當爲。補察之益盡于臣鄰，修省之誠協于上下。夫然後爲之君者，內無失德而聽斷益精，外無失政而照臨益廣，兼天下之視聽以作哲作謀，憲皇天之聰明以克明克類，信乎爲明明后，可以囘天眷而定邦家矣。夫以聖王之畏天若此其至，而著之謨訓者若此其嚴，羲和之玩天戒而侮聖言，尚何以容於斯世哉？

抑愚觀羲和之職，蓋唐虞命官之世，而顓頊氏重黎之遺也。啓征有扈，亦以威侮五行、怠棄三正言之。古人重天事尚矣。後是羲和無聞，周爲馮相、保章，列於天官之屬；漢以太史兼掌天官，事守益微。豈《胤征》之後，則遂削其世而貶其
translation_en:
…In fulfilling their duties [?], they uphold the law: they need only preserve the established statutes. If these statutes are not maintained, they will gather power to themselves and monopolize government, offending Heaven’s harmony above. To what lengths might they not go? Thus ministers do not lay responsibility for calamities and anomalies upon the state; they must reflect upon their own failure reverently to discharge their Heaven-appointed duties. They scrupulously observe established regulations and follow inherited institutions. In all that concerns serving the public and upholding the law, they dare harbor no intention of overstepping their bounds. Yet is merely keeping to established practice all that ministers should prize? They must foster a spirit of mutual admonition to remedy their ruler’s shortcomings, and personally display steadfast loyalty in performing the proper duties of their offices. When ministers close to the ruler fully contribute their corrective counsel, and those above and below unite in sincere self-cultivation and self-examination, only then will the ruler be free of failings in his inner virtue, becoming ever more discerning in hearing and deciding affairs; and free of failings in his outward government, extending his illuminating oversight ever further. Drawing upon the eyes and ears of all under Heaven, he achieves wisdom and sound deliberation; modeling himself upon august Heaven’s perceptiveness, he becomes discerning and able to distinguish things properly. Truly, as an enlightened sovereign, he can regain Heaven’s favor and secure the realm. Since the sage kings’ reverence for Heaven was so profound, and their recorded counsels and admonitions so stern, how could Xi and He, who treated Heaven’s warnings lightly and scorned the sages’ words, still be tolerated in this world?

Yet, in my humble view, the offices of Xi and He were hereditary appointments dating from the reigns of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, and a legacy of Chong and Li under Zhuanxu. When Qi campaigned against Youhu, he likewise charged them with contemptuously violating the Five Phases and negligently abandoning the Three Standards of the calendar. The ancients’ regard for celestial affairs was indeed longstanding. Thereafter, nothing more is heard of Xi and He. translation_en:
…their hereditary succession? As the world declined through successive ages, the concentrated dedication of the ancients vanished entirely. Those who reflect upon the ancients have only the sage kings’ counsels and admonitions remaining. Can we fail to ponder them?

Book of Odes

“In the tenth month, the crickets enter beneath our beds. We close the gaps in our houses and smoke out the rats; we stop up the north-facing windows and plaster the doors with earth. Ah, my wife and children! The year is about to turn: enter this house and dwell here. In the sixth month we eat bush cherries and wild grapes; in the seventh month we boil mallows and beans. In the eighth month we beat down the jujubes; in the tenth month we harvest rice. With it we make this spring wine, to help bring long life.”

Zheng Zhuangyan

Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: “The benevolent and righteous customs of the people of Bin, and the Duke of Zhou’s loyalty in indirectly admonishing his ruler, appear vividly before our eyes. Moreover, the writing is gentle, warm, sincere, and generous, deeply grasping the purport of the Book of Odes. It should be selected as a model.”

Associate Examiner Yan, Instructor, comments: “Warm, generous, refined, and correct: this is surely someone deeply versed in the teaching of the Odes. Select it.”

Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: “This ode reveals the Duke of Zhou’s loyalty to his ruler in more ways than one. The author understands that this constitutes the starting point of the Kingly Way. His future achievements in taking Heaven as his model can already be foreseen. It is entirely fitting to select this.”

Examiner Zhang, Left Mentor, comments: “Classical and elegant.”

Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher, comments: “There is exceptional grace and charm in the depiction of events.”

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
豳人以時豫事而長少交致其愛焉夫長者撫
下以即安而少者備物以致養豳俗之厚也詩
人詠之豈徒以其豫事之時耶且自后稷公劉
以來而豳之風化遠矣故即其居室飲食之間
而豳人之用情密矣自今觀之驗時物之變自
五月以至于十月則蟋蟀依人而寒氣總至矣
禦寒之備所宜周也修我墻屋穹斯窒之又從
而熏鼠焉塈茨其益完乎避彼北風向斯塞之
又從而墐戶焉外寒其少障乎室既葺矣而歲
===
事亦且改矣綏我婦子即我室家環堵之宮於
是乎胥宇三時之勤於是乎燠休一咨嗟之頃
而慈幼之仁不亦藹然可見哉興嗣歲之功自
正月以至于六月則二陰用事而百物嚮成矣
取物之節所宜知也六月而食鬱及薁七月而
烹葵及菽羞其新也而旨蓄因以具焉八月而
剥棗十月而穫稻薦其成也而蓋藏因以廣焉
稻既穫矣而釀事亦可給矣旨酒思柔嘉薦令
芳畀我尸賓而景福之是介寧我胡考而黃耇

punctuated: 豳人以時豫事，而長少交致其愛焉。夫長者撫下以即安，而少者備物以致養，豳俗之厚也。詩人詠之，豈徒以其豫事之時耶？且自后稷公劉以來，而豳之風化遠矣。故即其居室飲食之間，而豳人之用情密矣。自今觀之，驗時物之變，自五月以至于十月，則蟋蟀依人而寒氣總至矣。禦寒之備所宜周也。修我墻屋，穹斯窒之，又從而熏鼠焉，塈茨其益完乎？避彼北風，向斯塞之，又從而墐戶焉，外寒其少障乎？室既葺矣，而歲事亦且改矣。綏我婦子，即我室家，環堵之宮於是乎胥宇，三時之勤於是乎燠休。一咨嗟之頃，而慈幼之仁不亦藹然可見哉？興嗣歲之功，自正月以至于六月，則二陰用事而百物嚮成矣。取物之節所宜知也。六月而食鬱及薁，七月而烹葵及菽，羞其新也，而旨蓄因以具焉。八月而剥棗，十月而穫稻，薦其成也，而蓋藏因以廣焉。稻既穫矣，而釀事亦可給矣。旨酒思柔，嘉薦令芳，畀我尸賓而景福之是介，寧我胡考而黃耇
translation_en:
The people of Bin prepared their tasks in accordance with the seasons, and old and young alike thereby expressed their love for one another. The elders cared for those below them so that they might dwell in peace, while the young provided the things needed to nourish their elders: such was the generosity of Bin’s customs. When the poet sang of this, was it merely because they made their preparations at the proper time? Since the days of Hou Ji and Gong Liu, Bin’s moral influence had indeed extended far. Thus, even in their housing, food, and drink, the people of Bin showed the attentive care of their affections.

Looking at this now, we observe the changes in seasonal things: from the fifth month through the tenth, the crickets draw close to people, and the cold comes on in full force. Preparations against it should be thorough. We repair our walls and roofs, stop up their holes, and then smoke out the rats. Will not the plastering and thatching be more secure? To keep out the north wind, we block the windows and then seal the doors with earth. Will not the cold outside be somewhat checked? Once the house has been repaired, the labors of the year are also about to change. We settle our wives and children in comfort and enter our dwelling. Within its enclosing walls we now find a home; after the toil of three seasons, we now rest in warmth. In a single sigh of feeling, is not the benevolence of tender care for the young abundantly evident?

We undertake the work of the succeeding year. From the first month through the sixth, the second yin influence comes into operation, and all things approach maturity. The proper seasons for gathering produce should be understood. In the sixth month we eat bush cherries and wild grapes; in the seventh we cook mallows and beans. We offer what is fresh, and thereby lay in stores of delicious food. In the eighth month we beat down jujubes; in the tenth we harvest rice. We present the ripened produce, and thereby enlarge our reserves. Once the rice has been harvested, supplies for brewing are also assured. The fine wine is mellow, and the excellent offerings fragrant. We give them to the ancestral impersonator and the guests, thereby seeking great blessings; we bring peace to our aged elders, and venerable old age…

想哉夫以豳人之敏於趨時而勸於篤親如此

translation_en:
…and pray for venerable old age. In this single expression of praise and prayer, does not their reverence for the aged become vividly imaginable? The people of Bin were thus prompt in attending to the seasons and diligent in deepening affection for their kin. This reveals the virtue of the ancestral lords and the reason Zhou attained kingship—matters that all who inherit their charge ought to understand. I further venture to suggest that the poem “Seventh Month” contains several dozen major principles, yet the chief elements of the kingly Way are largely encompassed in these two: honoring the aged and cherishing the young. Thus Confucius drew on these when expressing his aspirations; Zengzi drew on them when discussing the principle of the measuring square; and Mengzi likewise drew on them when saying that the world could be turned in one's palm. Let those who subsequently discuss the kingly Way through the Odes seek its essentials here.
“Vast Heaven is bright, watching you as you go forth; vast Heaven is radiant, watching you as you roam.”
Tao Ze.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: The ministers of Zhou admonished one another to maintain reverence, to stand in awe of Heaven's scrutiny, and thereby to bring peace to the world. The candidates have been quite unaware of this meaning. This essay alone aptly conveys the luminous majesty of vast Heaven, standing awesomely before us. Reading it naturally inspires reverence. It is therefore selected for inclusion as a model for those who serve Heaven.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yan, Instructor: Candidates in the examination hall have often been constrained by the two words “bright” and “radiant”; their treatments are either prolix or obscure. This essay is concise, antique in style, lucid, and forceful, distinctly different from the others. It should be included as a model for the many scholars.

詩人言天監之有常所以示人當敬也夫人者
囿於天者也則夫日監在茲其孰能違之今夫
人之視天也以為有所及有所不及故其事天

夫天有運而無為惟其無為故能無乎不為蓋
不惟有以宰天下之動而實有以效天下之動

無與事焉然而天降明威非因出王而後有也
爾之出王而昊天之明其不隨在而見耶蓋日
與周旋有不自覺者矣人之有時而游衍不過
動息之間宜若天無聞知焉然而天有顯道非
待游衍而後彰也爾之游衍而昊天之旦其不

…[?] The wording is not prolix, yet the purport emerges of itself: this is a seasoned writer. It should be recorded to purge the baseness of scholars’ prevailing habits.
Examiner Zhang, Left Mentor, comments: This is someone who speaks well of Heaven.
Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher, comments: The treatment is very thorough and nuanced.
The poet speaks of the constancy of Heaven’s scrutiny to show that people ought to be reverent. Human beings exist within Heaven’s compass. Since its daily scrutiny is here among us, who can escape it? Nowadays people regard Heaven as reaching some places but not others. Thus, in serving Heaven, they suppose that they may either be reverent or dispense with reverence. Can this be called understanding Heaven? Heaven has visible manifestations but no bodily form. Precisely because it has no bodily form, there is nothing it does not embody. It thus not only unifies the forms of the myriad things, but also unifies their inner realities. Heaven moves, yet acts without deliberate effort. Precisely because it acts without deliberate effort, there is nothing it does not accomplish. It thus not only governs all movement under Heaven, but also brings all such movement to effect [?]. When people go forth, they cover no more than a few short steps; it might seem that Heaven has no part in the matter. Yet Heaven sends down its manifest majesty: this does not come into being only when one goes forth. When you go forth, does not the brightness of August Heaven reveal itself wherever you are? Indeed, people move within its presence daily without themselves being aware of it. When people roam at ease, this involves no more than movement and rest; it might seem that Heaven neither hears nor knows of it. Yet Heaven has its manifest Way: it does not wait until one roams at ease before becoming apparent. When you roam at ease, does not the radiance of August Heaven…

text:
即目而存耶蓋日與對越有不能外者矣人見
其昭昭之多也而不知其臨下之有赫也動與
之動焉靜與之靜焉而敢以馳驅爲也所以敬
忌天威者當何如哉人見其高高在上也而不
知旁燭之無疆也善必先知之不善必先知之
而敢以戲豫爲也所以奉若天道者當何如哉

即目而存耶？蓋日與對越，有不能外者矣。人見其昭昭之多也，而不知其臨下之有赫也。動與之動焉，靜與之靜焉，而敢以馳驅爲也？所以敬忌天威者，當何如哉？人見其高高在上也，而不知旁燭之無疆也。善必先知之，不善必先知之，而敢以戲豫爲也？所以奉若天道者，當何如哉？夫以天人之不相離如此，而天之方蹶，乃若無意於斯人，夫亦斯人之自叛其天耳矣。疾敬德以回天監，非吾人所當自力歟？周之臣工以是相戒，其意忠厚惻怛，而詞嚴誼正，凛然可畏。使閭井小民而知此，猶將日兢兢焉，如雷霆鬼神之臨乎其上。推其極，則聖人之「無貳爾心，上帝臨汝」，亦若是而已矣。聖澤未熄，而詩人之言每每近道，吾是以知《板》之後猶有《雲漢》《烝民》也。

translation_en:
…present before one’s very eyes? Indeed, each day we stand face to face with Heaven and cannot escape its presence. People see its abundant brightness, yet do not understand the awe-inspiring majesty with which it looks down upon them. When they move, it moves with them; when they rest, it rests with them. How, then, dare they rush about heedlessly? How ought they to revere and fear Heaven’s might! People see it high above, yet do not understand that its illumination reaches everywhere without limit. Goodness it invariably knows beforehand; wrongdoing it likewise knows beforehand. How, then, dare they indulge in idle amusement? How ought they to obey and follow Heaven’s Way!

Heaven and humanity are thus inseparable. Yet when Heaven brings upheaval, it seems to have no concern for these people. In truth, it is these people themselves who have betrayed their Heaven. Should we not exert ourselves to attend urgently and reverently to virtue, thereby turning Heaven’s regard back toward us? The ministers of Zhou admonished one another with these words. Their intent was loyal, generous, and deeply compassionate; their language was stern and their meaning upright, inspiring awe and fear. Even ordinary people in the villages, if they understood this, would live each day in trembling vigilance, as though thunder and spirits loomed above them. Carried to its utmost, this amounts to what the sage said: “Let your heart not be divided; the Lord on High looks down upon you.” It is no more than this. The influence of the sages had not yet died away, and the poets’ words repeatedly approached the Way. Thus I understand why, after “Admonition” (Ban), there were still poems such as “The Milky Way” (Yunhan) and “The Multitudes” (Zhengmin).

Spring and Autumn Annals

In the fifth month, on the guichou day, the duke met with the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Wei, and the Viscount of Ju, and they made a covenant at Jiantu. The duke paid court at the king’s place of residence. 〔Both passages.〕

春秋於王室之下勞，旣隱詞以全其名，復顯詞以正其本。夫舉動，人君之大節也。此周襄下勞晉侯之非，而聖人於踐土、王所之書，所以深致意歟？且夫禮莫大於分，分莫大於名，古今之通訓，不容僭差也。晉文城濮之功雖偉，然皆臣子之當為；周室之勢雖弱，則猶天下之共主也。若謂敵愾有錫為周之典，則因其獻俘而賜之弓矢可也，何至於屈萬乘之尊而親勞之耶？聖人脩經，蓋謂居尊臨卑，天地常經，不可易也。夫自周轍不西，而王室之存僅如綴旒，晉伯之强幾於改物，所恃以鎮服其心、不敢逞跋扈之威者，以天子之名尚在耳。此而夷之，則君臣之大倫
translation_en:
Bao Daoming 鮑道明

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, School Instructor: “Exhaustive yet tactful, pointed yet corrective, expansive and open [?], yet elegantly written. How profound his thought!”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Left Assistant Admonisher: “The meanings of the two commentaries are fundamentally connected; this composition grasps that connection.”

Comment by Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher: “This is precisely what the commentary means.”

In treating the Zhou king’s going down to commend a subordinate, the Spring and Autumn Annals first uses veiled wording to preserve his royal standing, then explicit wording to rectify the underlying principle. A ruler’s movements and actions are matters of great consequence. Was it not because King Xiang of Zhou acted wrongly in going down to commend the Marquis of Jin that the Sage expressed such profound concern through the entries concerning Jiantu and the king’s place of sojourn?

In ritual, nothing is greater than distinctions of station; in distinctions of station, nothing is greater than titles. This teaching holds for past and present alike and permits neither usurpation nor deviation. Although Duke Wen of Jin’s achievement at Chengpu was great, it was all within a subject’s duty. Although the power of the Zhou royal house was weak, its king remained the common sovereign of all under Heaven. If rewarding those who oppose the king’s enemies was an established Zhou practice, then granting bows and arrows upon the presentation of captives would have sufficed. Why go so far as to lower the dignity of the sovereign of ten thousand chariots by personally commending him? In editing the Classic, the Sage surely held that the exalted should preside over the lowly: this is an unalterable constant of Heaven and Earth.

Ever since the wheels of Zhou’s royal carriage ceased to turn westward, the royal house’s survival had been as precarious as a hanging tassel. The power of Jin’s hegemon came close to overturning the established order. What restrained his ambitions and kept him from unleashing his overbearing might was merely that the title of Son of Heaven still endured. If this distinction were leveled, then the great relationship between ruler and subject…

text:
不幾於滅息乎其何以教天下哉故特削其勞
伯之迹若曰襄未嘗與所以全名也此義行則
貴賤之志定而上下辨矣十二年王乃時巡諸
侯各朝于方岳周之常制不可違越也周襄踐
土之行實以勞晉之故諸侯衡雍之朝則非方
岳之禮也若謂江漢朝宗為臣之義則脩我王
章飭其侯度可也何至於舉享禮之嘉而野合
之耶聖人脩經盖謂位乎天德王者大閑不可
失也夫自三綱解紐而黍離東楚變為國風防
===
邑許田聘覲盡廢甚至於下堂而禮非復有先
王之舊者以天子之本弗正耳此而恕之則堂
陛之大體不幾於廢墜乎其何以訓方來哉故
特書曰朝于王所若曰所非其所所以正本也
此義行則人君之道修而鑒戒昭矣噫去實若
不貶矣然言有不貶而貶自見言所似不諱
矣然去實者不諱而諱猶存一諱一貶微而晦
志而婉夫子有心於周至是哉抑自弱之襄固
無望焉耳晉文賢伯也所望罄忠藎以扶其衰

punctuated:
不幾於滅息乎？其何以教天下哉？故特削其勞伯之迹，若曰襄未嘗與，所以全名也。此義行，則貴賤之志定而上下辨矣。
十二年，王乃時巡，諸侯各朝于方岳，周之常制，不可違越也。周襄踐土之行，實以勞晉之故；諸侯衡雍之朝，則非方岳之禮也。若謂江漢朝宗為臣之義，則脩我王章，飭其侯度可也，何至於舉享禮之嘉而野合之耶？聖人脩經，盖謂位乎天德，王者大閑，不可失也。夫自三綱解紐，而黍離東楚變為國風，防邑許田，聘覲盡廢，甚至於下堂，而禮非復有先王之舊者，以天子之本弗正耳。此而恕之，則堂陛之大體不幾於廢墜乎？其何以訓方來哉？故特書曰：「朝于王所。」若曰所非其所，所以正本也。此義行，則人君之道修而鑒戒昭矣。
噫！去實若不貶矣，然言有不貶而貶自見；言所似不諱矣，然去實者不諱而諱猶存。一諱一貶，微而晦，志而婉，夫子有心於周至是哉！抑自弱之襄，固無望焉耳。晉文，賢伯也，所望罄忠藎以扶其衰
translation_en:
…would it not verge on extinction? How, then, could this instruct all under Heaven? Thus the Sage specifically deleted the traces of the king’s rewarding the hegemon’s service, as though to say that King Xiang had never participated. This preserved his royal standing. When this principle prevails, the aspirations of noble and lowly become settled, and the distinction between superior and subordinate becomes clear.
Every twelve years the king would make a seasonal tour of inspection, and the feudal lords would each attend his court at the sacred mountain of their region. This was an established institution of Zhou that could not be transgressed. King Xiang of Zhou’s journey to Jiantu was actually undertaken to reward Jin’s service; the feudal lords’ audience at Hengyong was therefore not the prescribed ceremony at a regional sacred mountain. If one says that, just as the Jiang and Han rivers flow toward the sea, attending the royal court is a subject’s duty, then it would have sufficed to observe our royal statutes and enforce the regulations governing the lords. Why go so far as to take the splendid ceremonial of a court banquet and conduct it at an irregular gathering in the countryside? In revising the Classic, the Sage surely meant that occupying the position endowed with Heaven’s virtue entails fundamental restraints upon a king that must not be abandoned. Once the Three Bonds had come undone, “The Millet Droops” and “Dong Chu” [?] became Airs of the States; with Fangyi and Xutian [?], diplomatic visits and court audiences were entirely abandoned. Matters went so far that the king descended from his hall, and ritual no longer retained the old practices of the former kings—all because the Son of Heaven’s fundamental position had not been set right. If this were excused, would not the great order distinguishing the hall above from the steps below verge on collapse? How could it instruct future generations? Thus the Sage specifically wrote: “They attended court at the king’s location.” This was as though to say that the location was not his proper location, thereby rectifying the foundation. When this principle prevails, the way of the ruler is cultivated and the warning becomes clear.
Alas! Omitting the actual event appears to convey no censure, yet there are expressions that do not explicitly censure in which censure is self-evident. Saying “location” seems to conceal nothing, yet the omission of the actual event conceals nothing explicitly while concealment still remains. Concealment on the one hand and censure on the other: subtle and obscure, recording yet tactful. Such was the Master’s solicitude for Zhou! Yet nothing could really be hoped for from King Xiang, who weakened his own position. Duke Wen of Jin was a worthy hegemon; what was hoped of him was that he would devote all his loyalty to sustaining Zhou in its decline…

君處困而自棄也，可譏；臣謀國而弗善也，可責。夫國之所以能國者，以有君有臣也。匪是之選，胡然而君，胡然而臣哉？此夫子所以不滿於魯昭、季孫也。《易》有之：「困而不失其所亨」，言自强耳。是故甲兵弗繕，漕邑之處，所以興衛；禮幣行成，會稽之棲，所以昌越也。夫何魯昭之弗能自强
translation_en:
…Such was the hope. Yet when royal favor descended upon him, he complacently accepted the investiture without declining. How far did this depart from his words, “I bow to accept the command. I dare not be grasping, lest I fall and fail in my subordinate position”? Before long he requested a royal burial tunnel, thus disregarding his superior. Why, then, be surprised at the subsequent inquiry about the tripods? Thus, it was Xiang who honored Zhou, but Jin that weakened Zhou; it was Jin that secured the royal house of Zhou, but also Jin that brought about its decline. Devious and lacking rectitude—could one ever finish condemning this?
“In summer, the duke returned from Qi.” 〔Duke Zhao, year ten-[illegible].〕 “Wu attacked us.” 〔Duke Ai, eighth year.〕
Bi Zong.
Associate Examiner Chen, School Instructor, comments: “The wording is orderly and the spirit untrammeled. The conclusion is especially rich in lasting meaning. Reading it is enough to rouse even the fainthearted.”
Examiner Zhang, Left Admonisher, comments: “Careful and rigorous.”
Examiner Lun, Right Mentor, comments: “Elegant and vigorous.”
A ruler who abandons himself when in distress deserves criticism; a minister who plans poorly for the state deserves censure. What enables a state to function as a state is the presence of a ruler and ministers. Unless the right men are chosen, how can they be rulers, and how can they be ministers? This is why the Master was dissatisfied with Duke Zhao of Lu and Jisun. The Book of Changes says, “In distress, he does not lose that through which he finds success.” This speaks simply of strengthening oneself. Thus, with armor and weapons unrepaired, residence in the town of Cao became the means of reviving Wei; with ritual gifts offered to negotiate peace, refuge at Kuaiji became the means of bringing prosperity to Yue. Why, then, was Duke Zhao of Lu unable to strengthen himself…

text:
耶蓋魯之於晋三見卻於河上兩拘留於國中
窘辱備至其目中之無魯也亦旣已久矣使昭
而文公焉而勾踐焉則興憂啓憤之餘魯國其
將有振乎胡為泄泄然甘耻辱而不辭徒能從
事於威儀之末而不知立身之大本之不可緩
也發聲徵色而弗喻困心衡慮而弗作斯則下
愚而已爾其於大易之訓何如耶他日乾侯之
孫亦其自貽之感也德則弗競其誰之尤哉故
夫子書至晋而諱見止者其貶之深矣詩有之
===
子曰有奔奏予曰有禦侮言得人耳是故國斃
不從華元之義所以平楚背城借一國佐之忠
所以强齊也夫何季孫之無益於人國耶彼吳
師之至雖進次於泗上猶一夕而三遷四鄙甫
侵其患之在魯也猶未及虧矣使季孫而華元
焉而國佐焉則忠詞真氣之發吳兵其敢自久
乎胡為瑣瑣然盟城下而不耻徒知偷安於息
肩之圖而罔識辱國之大之為可羞也宵攻之
計弗之從棄國之言弗之聽斯則具臣而已爾

translation_en:
…? In Lu’s dealings with Jin, its ruler was turned back three times at the Yellow River and detained twice within Jin’s borders, suffering every kind of humiliation and distress. Jin had long ceased to regard Lu as a state of any consequence. Had Duke Zhao acted like Duke Wen or Goujian, might Lu not have revived after anxiety and indignation had stirred him to action? Why did he remain so indolent, accepting disgrace without protest, capable only of attending to the minutiae of ceremonial deportment, yet unaware that the great foundations of personal conduct admitted no delay? Though admonition sounded in voices and appeared in countenances, he did not understand; though his mind was distressed and his deliberations thwarted, he did not rise to action. He was simply one of the utterly foolish. How did this accord with the teachings of the great Book of Changes? His subsequent exile at Ganhou was also a consequence he brought upon himself [?]. Since his virtue proved unequal to the task, whom could he blame? Thus, when the Master recorded his arrival in Jin but avoided explicitly recording his detention, the censure was profound indeed.
The Book of Odes says: “You say there are men who hasten to your service; I say there are men who ward off insult.” This speaks simply of obtaining the right men. Thus Hua Yuan’s righteousness, expressed in his resolve that his state would perish rather than submit, enabled him to make peace with Chu; Guo Zuo’s loyalty, expressed in his resolve to make one final stand with the city walls at his back, enabled him to strengthen Qi. Why, then, was Jisun of no benefit to the state he served? When the army of Wu arrived, although it advanced and encamped on the Si River, it still moved camp three times in a single night. Its invasion of the outlying districts had only just begun, and the danger it posed had not yet inflicted substantial damage on Lu. Had Jisun acted like Hua Yuan or Guo Zuo, would Wu’s troops have dared prolong their stay once his loyal words and sincere spirit were displayed? Why did he act so meanly, concluding a covenant beneath the city walls without shame, knowing only how to secure momentary ease through a plan to lay down his burdens, yet failing to recognize the shame of so grave a humiliation of his state? He would not follow the plan for a night attack, nor would he heed the proposal to abandon the capital. He was merely a minister who filled an office. …

諱與盟者深責之矣是故觀于斯者可以起懦
