…How does this measure up to the Poetry of Zhou? His later encounter with Yue was also a trouble he brought upon himself [?]. If his planning was unsound, how could the outcome be good? Thus, when the Master wrote “attacked us” but avoided mentioning participation in the covenant, he was expressing profound censure. Those who consider this can be roused from cowardice and strengthened in integrity; they can ensure that rulers act as rulers and ministers as ministers, so that no state under Heaven falls into ruin. How great is the sage’s teaching! Even so, Zhao was certainly at fault, but the one who humiliated Zhao trusted the accusations of the barbarians and severed the friendship between brother states. Duke Zhao of Jin was like Duke Zhao of Lu: how could he restore the flourishing rule of Dukes Wen and Xiang? Jisun was certainly culpable, but the one who invited humiliation failed to employ the worthies of the sage’s school, indulged the arbitrary power of the Three Huan lineages, and heeded them alone. Jisun’s ruler was like Duke Ai’s minister [?]: how could he bring peace to the Lu of the Duke of Zhou? There is indeed good reason why the Doctrine of the Mean values banishing slander and the Great Learning values employing the right people.
Record of Rites
The Son of Heaven performs the spring yue sacrifice separately [?], and the summer di, autumn chang, and winter zheng sacrifices as combined ancestral sacrifices. Among the feudal lords, one who performs the yue does not perform the di; one who performs the di does not perform the chang; one who performs the chang does not perform the zheng; and one who performs the zheng does not perform the yue. The feudal lords perform the yue separately [?]; for the di, they alternate a separate sacrifice [?] with a combined sacrifice; the chang and zheng are combined sacrifices.

text:
意尤善
考試官右諭德倫批整潔
記者詳言時祭之隆殺所以辨尊卑之分也夫
天子諸侯之分不同而祭亦因之以異也隆殺
之辨其可弗愼矣乎且夫禮有五經莫重於祭
而礿禘嘗烝則時祭之行乎宗廟者也自其主
之各享於本廟也而礿斯名焉自其主之合食
於太廟也而祫斯名焉由天子而視諸侯上則
七廟之流光下則萬邦之助祭宗廟之禮得以
===
自盡其所欲爲者矣是故礿非不可以祫也順
發生之時無取於備物致精禋之薦不嫌於儉
親故省而從礿非薄也禘嘗烝則皆祫矣物以
漸而成見天時之咸若享以漸而豐昭民力之
普存故歲而三祫非後也夫祫之爲體重矣三
時用之礿之爲事輕矣歲一行之天子之禮之
致隆夫豈强爲哉其分則然也由諸侯而視天
子內崇五廟之親外謹維藩之度宗廟之禮時
有所屈而不容僭差矣是故有事于夏秋之廟

記者詳言時祭之隆殺，所以辨尊卑之分也。夫天子諸侯之分不同，而祭亦因之以異也。隆殺之辨，其可弗愼矣乎？且夫禮有五經，莫重於祭，而礿禘嘗烝，則時祭之行乎宗廟者也。自其主之各享於本廟也，而礿斯名焉；自其主之合食於太廟也，而祫斯名焉。由天子而視諸侯，上則七廟之流光，下則萬邦之助祭，宗廟之禮得以自盡其所欲爲者矣。是故礿非不可以祫也，順發生之時，無取於備物，致精禋之薦，不嫌於儉親，故省而從礿，非薄也。禘嘗烝則皆祫矣，物以漸而成，見天時之咸若；享以漸而豐，昭民力之普存，故歲而三祫，非後也。夫祫之爲體重矣，三時用之；礿之爲事輕矣，歲一行之。天子之禮之致隆，夫豈强爲哉？其分則然也。由諸侯而視天子，內崇五廟之親，外謹維藩之度，宗廟之禮時有所屈，而不容僭差矣。是故有事于夏秋之廟，
translation_en:
…the idea is especially good.
Examiner Lun, Right Mentor, comments: “Orderly and polished.”
The compiler explains in detail the greater and lesser elaboration of the seasonal sacrifices in order to distinguish the respective stations of superior and inferior. The Son of Heaven and the feudal lords occupy different stations, and their sacrifices accordingly differ. Can one fail to exercise care in distinguishing these degrees of elaboration? Ritual has five principal divisions, of which none is weightier than sacrifice. The yue, di, chang, and zheng are the seasonal sacrifices performed in the ancestral temples. When each ancestral spirit tablet receives offerings separately in its own temple, the designation yue applies; when the tablets share offerings in the Grand Ancestral Temple, the designation xia, or joint sacrifice, applies.
Consider the feudal lords from the position of the Son of Heaven: above, the seven ancestral temples transmit their glory; below, the myriad states assist with the sacrifices. He can therefore fulfill all that he wishes to perform in the rites of the ancestral temples. Thus, it is not that the yue sacrifice cannot take the form of a joint sacrifice. Following the season when things emerge and grow, it does not require a full complement of offerings. In presenting offerings of pure devotion, there is no objection to frugality toward one’s kin [?]. Thus, reducing the ceremony and following the yue form does not constitute meagerness. The di, chang, and zheng, however, all take the form of joint sacrifices. As the products gradually mature, they manifest complete conformity with Heaven’s seasons; as the offerings gradually become abundant, they display the full availability of the people’s labor. Thus, holding three joint sacrifices in a year is not being behind [?].
The form of the joint sacrifice is weighty, and it is employed in three seasons; the observance of the yue is less weighty, and it is performed once a year. Is the utmost elaboration of the Son of Heaven’s rites something artificially imposed? His station makes it so. Consider the Son of Heaven from the position of the feudal lords: within, they honor their kin in five ancestral temples; without, they carefully observe the limits proper to their role as bulwarks of the realm. Their ancestral temple rites must at times be curtailed, and no presumptuous departure from their station is permitted. Thus, when performing services in the ancestral temples in summer and autumn…

text:
則禴可以無禘而禘可以無嘗也有事于冬春
之朝則嘗可以無烝而烝可以無禴也歲事其
能以畢修乎禴與嘗烝隨時而植祫焉天子所
同也夏祭之禘間歲而植祫焉天子所異也品
節其能以無别乎夫廟祀有國之重也急王事
而有所缺禘祭三時之始也避王尊而有所間
諸侯之禮之降殺又豈強為哉其分則然也夫
以孝享之典而尊王之敎寓焉仁之至義之盡
非先王其孰能盡制如此者乎雖然夫祭與其
===
敬不足而禮有餘也不若禮不足而敬有餘也
心之能敬雖殺隆也犯分以為悅黷祀以為勤
暴殄天物以為美觀而敬心益微神之顧享未
可必也烏在其能隆是故敬者仁義之維而禮
之實也
其言也約而達微而臧罕譬而喻可謂繼
志矣

translation_en:
…then the yue sacrifice may be performed without the di, and the di without the chang. When there is service at court in winter or spring, the chang may be performed without the zheng, and the zheng without the yue. Can the year's observances all be fully performed? In the yue, chang, and zheng sacrifices, a combined ancestral sacrifice is instituted in its proper season: in this the practice is the same as the Son of Heaven's. In the summer di sacrifice, a combined ancestral sacrifice is instituted in alternate years: in this the practice differs from the Son of Heaven's. Can the prescribed gradations admit no distinctions? Ancestral temple sacrifices are a weighty responsibility for those who possess a state, yet some are omitted because the king's affairs take precedence. The di sacrifice begins the observances of the three seasons, yet it is performed at intervals out of deference to the king's exalted status. Are these reductions in the rites of the feudal lords arbitrarily imposed? Their allotted station makes them so. The teaching of reverence for the king is thus embodied in the rules for filial offerings. This is benevolence at its utmost and righteousness fully realized. Who but the former kings could have devised so complete a system?
Nevertheless, in sacrifice, deficient ceremony with abundant reverence is better than abundant ceremony with deficient reverence. When the heart is reverent, even reduced observances are exalted. But if one transgresses the bounds of one's station to give pleasure, treats excessive sacrifices as diligence, and recklessly wastes Heaven's gifts to create a splendid spectacle, the reverent heart grows ever fainter. Whether the spirits will deign to accept the offerings cannot be assured. Wherein, then, lies the grandeur of such observances? Reverence is therefore the bond of benevolence and righteousness, and the substance of ritual.

He Ge.

…the subtlety of enabling others to carry forward one’s purpose. The exposition is precise, incisive, and rich in meaning. Writers like this are exceedingly rare in the examination hall. Admiration indeed, admiration indeed!

Examiner Zhang, Left Admonisher, comments: This is someone who does more than merely concern himself with words.

Examiner Lun, Right Mentor, comments: Ample, yet free of overgrowth.

Only when the teacher fully employs the methods of skillful guidance do learners obtain their benefit. Between teaching and learning, what is difficult is for minds to meet. How could the benefit of inward understanding depend upon a profusion of words? The Record of Rites says that a good teacher enables others to carry forward his purpose. But how can that purpose be carried forward? Teaching certainly cannot dispense with words, yet neither does it rely exclusively upon them. Instruction through words penetrates but shallowly; a meeting of minds achieves a deep accord. When understanding is transmitted from mind to mind, the teacher’s purpose can be carried forward.

Thus, when concise words elucidate principles, which are grasped with the mind without need of elaborate explanation, an enduring savor remains, and the import of the meaning can be apprehended. Is this not being concise yet comprehensible? When gentle expressions make goodness clear, awakening understanding in the mind without need of insistent haranguing, a living responsiveness is set in motion, and the whereabouts of goodness can be traced through reflection. Is this not being subtle yet excellent? As for the use of analogies, the words of comparison are few, but their power to move is profound. The very act of comparing things and grouping like with like provides scope for developing their implications fully and extending understanding to related matters. To use few analogies yet make oneself understood is simply to nourish one mind with another, drawing upon its existing understanding to enlighten it.

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
費辭而意足焉體諸心而知其要自不騖於多
岐矣高論失之峻則學者之志沮惟夫微而臧
也不下帶而道存焉明諸心而知所往自不苦
於難入矣廣譬失之誣則學者之志荒惟夫罕
譬而喻也引而伸之足以滿其所欲聞迎而解
之足以發其所深省此以心感彼以心應蓋有
渙然氷釋而怡然理順者繼志之學不於此而
得之乎否則諄諄以誨而心之扞格者自如也
烏得爲善教哉雖然此聖門教人之法也夫子
===
未嘗無言乃曰予欲無言蓋不得已而言其言
曲而中矣啓憤發悱反三隅則復之此其節度
也後世儒者授受言益多道益隱其心固未嘗
有以自得而學者又曷從而求之彼異端乃竊
聖門之緒餘而用之曰正容以悟之使人之意
也消再變而爲禪解機鋒之學則又似是而非
所當辭而闢焉者也
第貳塲
論

punctuated:
費辭而意足焉，體諸心而知其要，自不騖於多岐矣。高論失之峻，則學者之志沮；惟夫微而臧也，不下帶而道存焉，明諸心而知所往，自不苦於難入矣。廣譬失之誣，則學者之志荒；惟夫罕譬而喻也，引而伸之，足以滿其所欲聞；迎而解之，足以發其所深省。此以心感，彼以心應，蓋有渙然氷釋而怡然理順者。繼志之學，不於此而得之乎？否則，諄諄以誨，而心之扞格者自如也，烏得爲善教哉？雖然，此聖門教人之法也。夫子未嘗無言，乃曰：「予欲無言。」蓋不得已而言，其言曲而中矣。啓憤發悱，反三隅則復之，此其節度也。後世儒者授受，言益多，道益隱；其心固未嘗有以自得，而學者又曷從而求之？彼異端乃竊聖門之緒餘而用之，曰：「正容以悟之，使人之意也消。」再變而爲禪解機鋒之學，則又似是而非，所當辭而闢焉者也。
第貳塲
論
translation_en:
…without expending many words, the meaning is fully conveyed. By taking it to heart and grasping its essentials, learners naturally cease to pursue a multitude of divergent paths. When lofty discourse errs by being too forbidding, learners lose heart. Only when instruction is subtle yet sound does the Way remain present in words that reach no farther than the sash. Understanding it in their hearts and knowing where to proceed, learners naturally cease to find entry difficult. When abundant analogies err by being misleading, learners’ purposes become unfocused. Only when analogies are few yet illuminating can their implications be extended far enough to satisfy what learners wish to hear, and their difficulties met and resolved sufficiently to awaken deep reflection. One heart moves another, and that heart responds: doubts dissolve like melting ice, and principles fall pleasantly into order. Is this not how one acquires the learning that carries forward the teacher’s purposes? Otherwise, however earnestly one instructs, the obstruction in the learner’s heart remains unchanged. How could that count as good teaching?
Nevertheless, this is the method of instruction practiced in the school of the Sage. The Master was never without words, yet he said, “I wish to be without words.” He spoke only when he could not do otherwise, and his words, though indirect, hit their mark. He opened the understanding of those struggling to comprehend and helped those struggling to express themselves; he continued instruction when they could infer the other three corners from one. Such was his measured approach. In later generations, as Confucian scholars transmitted and received instruction, their words grew ever more numerous and the Way ever more obscure. Since they themselves had never inwardly grasped it, where could learners turn to seek it? Those of heterodox teachings appropriated remnants of the Sage’s teaching and employed them, saying, “Compose your countenance to awaken them, causing people’s intentions to melt away.” [?] Transformed yet again into the learning of Chan interpretations and pointed verbal exchanges, this appeared correct but was false, and ought to be rejected and refuted.
Second Session
Discourse

…viewed thus, the mandate determining rise and decline admits not a hair’s breadth between them, yet Heaven’s benevolent concern [?] is always apparent before events first show their signs. Viewed in its smaller manifestations, when an ordinary man or woman cries out over an injustice [?], Heaven will stir up violent winds and send down frost on their account. How much more so when the suffering is twofold, fivefold, tenfold, a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or ten thousandfold greater! What spontaneously draws together the love of all under Heaven is harmony at its utmost; what gathers the resentment of all under Heaven in anguished distress is discord at its utmost. To utmost harmony, the harmonious vital energies of Heaven and Earth respond; to utmost discord, their contrary vital energies respond. The Book of Changes says: “Heaven displays images, revealing good and ill fortune.” Could the causes of calamities and auspicious signs be mere chance?

I have considered this: auspicious stars, felicitous clouds, sweet springs, and numinous fungi are the outward manifestations of good fortune; seasonable weather, abundant harvests, and the well-being and plenty of people and things are its substance. Sounds from Heaven, earthquakes, anomalies among creatures, and prodigies among humans are the outward manifestations of calamity; untimely floods and droughts, impoverishment of the people, and the rise of banditry are its substance. Where the substance of good fortune exists without its outward manifestations, this does not prevent the age from being well governed. How much more so when manifestation and substance arrive together! Where the substance of calamity exists without its outward manifestations, this does not prevent it from being a sign of fault. How much more so when manifestation and substance arrive together!

People are born with desires, yet cannot fulfill them themselves. When their deprivation accumulates until they lose their proper place and can no longer sustain their lives, the vital energy of their sorrow and suffering assails the harmony of yin and yang and disorders the essence of Heaven and Earth. Pent up, it becomes pestilential affliction; surging forth, it becomes ominous vapors. There is something inevitable in this mechanism of sympathetic response. Formerly, when the Duke of Zhou established Zhou [?], he allowed ordinary people to voice criticism, and further said: “When the common people resent you and revile you, then greatly revere virtue in your own conduct.” Why did the Duke of Zhou welcome criticism and abuse? 故民有恃也彼其竢之而未至明之而弗徵稽
之而弗究其竟恃之而莫之能必也則以夫未
定之天而忽其昭示之變非所與論於天人之
際也且夫三才奚自而立耶根諸鴻濛而判焉
者也天地之大德曰生而其所欲生者蓋莫甚
於人是萬物之靈而天地所依以立焉者也天
地不能自主其民而付之大君大君者天地人
之間者也是其類不離乎形化而其威命靈爽
侔乎造化者也苟克奉天子民則薄海內外戴
===
之如天地如其不然則天人亦將交去之是天
地也人也大君也相依為命焉者也人銷物盡
天地且迹熄焉高而無民於君人奚有哉凡君
民之交也以言而天人之交也以意天無心亦
無言而意安從生蓋聞之曰天視聽自我民視
聽天明畏自我民明威欲知天意之所在其惟
民心乎夫天居高聽卑是故遠而近也體物而
不遺是故微而彰也陟降厥士是故疎而不漏
也因材而篤是故善應而不宰也故自其大者

…Thus the people have something on which to rely. Those who wait for it without its arriving, seek to clarify it without obtaining confirmation, and investigate it without reaching a conclusion ultimately rely on something of which they can have no certainty. Thus, because Heaven seems indeterminate, they disregard the changes through which it plainly gives warning. Such people are not fit to discuss the relationship between Heaven and humanity.

Moreover, whence did the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—arise? They were rooted in primordial chaos and became differentiated from it. The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life-giving; and among those whom they wish to bring to life, surely none matters more than humanity. Humans are the most spiritually endowed of the myriad beings, and those upon whom Heaven and Earth depend for their standing. Heaven and Earth cannot themselves govern their people, so they entrust them to the great ruler. The great ruler stands between Heaven, Earth, and humanity. In his kind he remains subject to bodily transformation, yet his commanding authority and spiritual intelligence match the creative workings of nature. If he can serve Heaven and cherish the people as his children, all within and beyond the seas will revere him as they do Heaven and Earth. Otherwise, Heaven and humanity alike will abandon him. Thus Heaven and Earth, humanity, and the great ruler depend upon one another for their existence. Were humans to vanish and other beings to perish, even the traces of Heaven and Earth would disappear. What could a ruler possess, however exalted, if he had no people?

Communication between ruler and people takes place through words; communication between Heaven and humanity takes place through intent. Yet Heaven has neither a mind nor words: whence, then, does its intent arise? I have heard it said: “Heaven sees and hears through what our people see and hear; Heaven makes manifest its awe-inspiring power through what our people make manifest and regard with awe.” If one wishes to know where Heaven’s intent lies, surely it is in the people’s hearts! Heaven dwells on high but hears those below; thus, though distant, it is near. It gives substance to things and leaves none out; thus, though subtle, it is manifest. It ascends and descends in its affairs [?]; thus, though its net is wide-meshed, nothing escapes. It nurtures each according to its nature; thus it responds aptly without acting as a master. Therefore, beginning with the greatest…

text:
怨咨猶有泄也後世有監謗焉者有嚴刑峻法
使民敢怒不敢言焉者夫蓄毒於腹心而無異
故此其為變必不為恒證而遂為癰疽亦明矣
為國者將銷患於未形而可使厚蓄之毒而濱
於潰决也哉君人擅國之名寵居可致之位操
可致之權朝令而夕化夕禁而朝戢修之乎廟
廊之上動之乎氣機之間於以銷未形之患宜
無難者是故省刑罰薄稅斂恤煢獨雪寃抑罷
興作蠲煩苛戮貪酷進忠良釋逋負綏携貳問
===
民疾苦布德行惠此數者仁民之政之大端也
推誠而行之覈其實而致之民使夫困者蘇踣
者起流離瑣尾者還定而安集瘡痏殄瘁者完
好而充悅和氣融液天心克享變災為祥易危
為安在反覆掌間耳孔子稱一日克己復禮天
下歸仁焉宋景公三善言而熒惑退舍况善政
實及民者哉故曰動民以行不以言應天以實
不以文側身脩行之君率曰此道故能自求多
福而統會天人也世主不知出此往往玩天之

怨咨猶有泄也。後世有監謗焉者，有嚴刑峻法使民敢怒不敢言焉者。夫蓄毒於腹心而無異故，此其為變，必不為恒證而遂為癰疽，亦明矣。為國者將銷患於未形，而可使厚蓄之毒而濱於潰决也哉？君人擅國之名寵，居可致之位，操可致之權，朝令而夕化，夕禁而朝戢。修之乎廟廊之上，動之乎氣機之間，於以銷未形之患，宜無難者。是故省刑罰，薄稅斂，恤煢獨，雪寃抑，罷興作，蠲煩苛，戮貪酷，進忠良，釋逋負，綏携貳，問民疾苦，布德行惠，此數者仁民之政之大端也。

推誠而行之，覈其實而致之民，使夫困者蘇，踣者起，流離瑣尾者還定而安集，瘡痏殄瘁者完好而充悅，和氣融液，天心克享。變災為祥，易危為安，在反覆掌間耳。孔子稱：「一日克己復禮，天下歸仁焉。」宋景公三善言而熒惑退舍，况善政實及民者哉？故曰：「動民以行，不以言；應天以實，不以文。」側身脩行之君，率曰此道，故能自求多福而統會天人也。世主不知出此，往往玩天之

…resentment and lamentation still had an outlet. In later ages, some rulers kept watch for criticism; others imposed harsh punishments and severe laws, making the people dare to feel anger but not to speak. If poison accumulates in the belly and heart without any outward disturbance, it is clear that, when it produces a change, this will not take the form of ordinary symptoms but will develop directly into abscesses and ulcers. Those who govern a state seek to eliminate troubles before they take shape: can they allow poison to accumulate densely until it is on the verge of bursting forth? A ruler possesses the prestige and honor of sovereign authority, occupies a position from which results can be achieved, and wields the power to achieve them. An order issued in the morning brings change by evening; a prohibition imposed at evening brings restraint by morning. By setting matters right at court and acting upon the subtle workings of change, he should have no difficulty eliminating troubles before they take shape. Thus, reducing punishments, lightening taxes, caring for the forlorn and solitary, redressing injustice and oppression, halting construction projects, abolishing burdensome exactions, executing the corrupt and cruel, promoting the loyal and worthy, remitting arrears, pacifying the estranged and wavering, inquiring into the people's hardships, and extending virtue and beneficence—these are the principal measures of government that treats the people humanely.

Carry these measures out with sincerity, examine their actual effects, and bring their benefits to the people. Let those in distress recover and those who have fallen rise again; let the displaced and downtrodden return to settled homes and gather in security; let the wounded and exhausted become whole, well provided for, and content. Then harmonious influences will flow freely, and Heaven will be pleased. Turning calamity into good fortune and danger into security will be as easy as turning over one's hand. Confucius said: “If for a single day one overcomes the self and returns to ritual propriety, all under Heaven will turn to humaneness.” Three good utterances by Duke Jing of Song caused Mars to retreat from its celestial lodge; how much more effective must good government be when it actually reaches the people! translation_en:
…Heaven’s might, and deceive the people to gratify themselves. If they disregard Heaven’s might and deceive the people to gratify themselves, a spirit of arrogance and carelessness will inevitably enter their hearts. Once such a spirit enters, arguments marked by flattery, treachery, clever disputation, and ruthless severity will inevitably answer it. When flattering arguments prevail, the ruler’s virtue is impaired; when arguments for ruthless severity prevail, the circumstances and feelings of those below are shut out; when clever disputation prevails, the correct Way is destroyed; and when treacherous arguments prevail, expedient schemes are devised. If these four courses are followed, oppressive government will increase daily, falsification and deception will grow ever worse, the people’s livelihood will become ever more straitened, and the benevolent concern of Heaven will be increasingly spurned. How long could it be before all sink together into ruin?

Alas! Heaven established sovereigns, kings, lords, and dukes, supporting them with great officers, teachers, and leaders. Its greater purpose was to have them govern all things on Heaven’s behalf; its lesser purpose was still to have them tend and guide the people, allowing them to sustain themselves and multiply. Even if they cannot accomplish this, if instead they alienate their people and thereby cut themselves off from Heaven, what can be done about them? Nevertheless, Master Dong said: “Unless an age is utterly without the Way, Heaven wishes to support it and preserve it in peace.” Thus, in a single moment of awakening, the pivotal movement toward order or disorder can be reversed. This, too, is among the subtlest aspects of the relationship between Heaven and humanity. It is why loyal ministers and men of high purpose remain so earnestly concerned and cannot desist.

考試官右諭德倫　批〔典實中有餘味得體〕
伏以
諏經下學日降晉接之規
稅駕西成天普霈雲之惠動遵軌物義表
明良拜手
同遊顧省循而曷稱捫心
飫賜知踴躍以奚勝恭惟
皇帝陛下
欽明文思安安
punctuated:
李重

同考試官訓導王批：臣子對君之辭，最不易言。是作頌而諷，典而不俗，麗而不縟，可錄也。

同考試官教諭楊批：寫無逸、豳風之意，宛然可見。真得人臣告君之體，非但工於四六者。

考試官左贊善張批：敷揚君臣相悅之意殆盡，且麗而有則，其盛世之音乎！

考試官右諭德倫批：典實中有餘味，得體。

伏以：講經下學，日隆晉接之規；稅駕西成，天普需雲之惠。動遵軌物，義表明良。拜手同遊，顧省循而曷稱；捫心飫賜，知踴躍以奚勝。恭惟皇帝陛下，欽明文思，安安……
translation_en:
Li Zhong

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Assistant Instructor: A subject’s words addressed to his ruler are exceedingly difficult to compose. This piece offers praise while conveying admonition; it is classically grounded without being commonplace, elegant without excessive ornament. It merits inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: The meaning of “Against Luxurious Ease” (Wuyi) and the “Airs of Bin” (Binfeng) is vividly apparent in this writing. It truly achieves the proper manner for a subject addressing his ruler, going beyond mere skill in four- and six-character parallel prose.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Left Admonisher: It develops almost exhaustively the theme of mutual delight between ruler and ministers. Moreover, its elegance observes due restraint. Surely this is the voice of a flourishing age!

Comment by Examiner Lun, Right Mentor: Its classical substance leaves a lingering savor; its manner is appropriate.

I humbly submit: In having the classics expounded and pursuing learning from its foundations, you daily enhance the practice of receiving your ministers. In halting your carriage amid the autumn harvest, you extend everywhere Heaven’s bounty, like the clouds of the hexagram Waiting, which promise nourishment. Your every action accords with established norms; its significance manifests an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers. Bowing with hands joined, we accompany you on your excursion; yet, examining ourselves, how could we be worthy of this honor? Searching our hearts as we feast upon your gifts, how could we contain our exuberant joy?

We reverently contemplate Your Majesty the Emperor: reverent and discerning, accomplished and thoughtful, naturally at ease in these virtues…

敬止緝熙穆穆
無偏無黨建極錫民
惟時惟幾敕天基命
念王業艱難之自知小人稼穡之依
先天下以憂民後日中而旰食惟周公之進
戒悉心于無逸一篇迨孔子之刪詩正變
于豳風七月其效極於祈天永命其事詳
於育物授時盖帝王之道在憂勤率先民
務故詩書之言相表裏妙契
淵衷南郊屢

宮壖之隙實惟鉤盾之遺建
帝社
帝稷之壇春秋躬祀集侯疆侯以之衆逺近子
來我理我疆力盡南東之畆
時遊時豫民無警蹕之勞爰開
絳節之朝少便
翠華之駐

punctuated: 敬止緝熙穆穆，無偏無黨，建極錫民；惟時惟幾，敕天基命。念王業艱難之自，知小人稼穡之依；先天下以憂民，後日中而旰食。惟周公之進戒，悉心于無逸一篇；迨孔子之刪詩，正變于豳風七月。其效極於祈天永命，其事詳於育物授時。盖帝王之道在憂勤，率先民務，故詩書之言相表裏，妙契淵衷。南郊屢詔於勸耕，西苑肇修於觀稼。繄彼宮壖之隙，實惟鉤盾之遺。建帝社帝稷之壇，春秋躬祀；集侯疆侯以之衆，逺近子來。我理我疆，力盡南東之畆；時遊時豫，民無警蹕之勞。爰開絳節之朝，少便翠華之駐。
translation_en:
…reverently abiding in the highest good, continuing in luminous virtue, solemn and majestic. Without partiality or faction, Your Majesty establishes the supreme standard and bestows it upon the people; attentive to the proper moment and the smallest incipient change, you heed Heaven and consolidate its mandate. You reflect upon the hardships from which the royal enterprise arose and understand the farming upon which ordinary people depend. Before all others under Heaven, you take thought for the people; only after midday do you take your belated meal. When the Duke of Zhou offered his admonitions, he devoted his whole attention to the chapter Against Idleness. When Confucius edited the Odes, he distinguished the orthodox and altered forms in Seventh Month of the Airs of Bin [?]. Their ultimate efficacy lies in seeking from Heaven an enduring mandate; their practical details concern nurturing living things and communicating the proper seasons for work. For the way of emperors and kings consists in anxious diligence and taking the lead in the people's labors. Thus the words of the Odes and the Documents complement one another and accord wondrously with Your Majesty's profound intentions.
At the southern suburban altar, you have repeatedly issued edicts encouraging agriculture; in the Western Park, you have initiated works for observing the crops. That open space beside the palace precincts is indeed a surviving tract under the Goudun, the office responsible for imperial gardens. You have built altars to the imperial gods of soil and grain, personally offering sacrifices in spring and autumn. You have assembled the multitude who mark out the fields and undertake their cultivation [?]; from near and far they come like children to a parent. “We put our fields in order; we mark out their boundaries”: their strength is fully devoted to the southward- and eastward-facing acres. Your Majesty's excursions and recreation take place at the proper times, and the people bear no burden of clearing the roads for the imperial passage. Here a court is opened for the crimson standards, affording a convenient stopping place for the kingfisher-feather imperial banners…

translation_en:
… The hall is named Wuyi, “Without Ease”: morning and night, Your Majesty personally labors for the people. The pavilion bears the inscription Binfeng, “Airs of Bin”: following the rhythms of yin and yang, you issue seasonal ordinances. The northern lodge encompasses all the work of sericulture; the western pavilion overlooks the yard of gathered stalks [?]. Yu’s irrigation channels are kept flowing; Yao’s thatch remains untrimmed. The foundations of the dynasty are laid here, beside the old palace of the cultured ancestor. The teachings of the Classics are fields to be cultivated; upon the walls are displayed the inspired writings of Emperor Xian. The sacred learning of predecessor and successor follows a single standard, brilliantly bequeathing abundance to posterity. Thus the two steles bearing imperial compositions, one to the left and one to the right, proclaim and honor that legacy without end.

In this season of autumn, you graciously come to view the ripening of the myriad precious crops. Your ceremonial attendants hasten forward; the farmers await your visit. Auspicious clouds support the imperial carriage, and the call to clear the way is heard from the ninefold palace. Rich dew moistens its bells, and your dragon radiance is beheld at close quarters. A summons is conveyed to the chief ministers, who sit to discuss the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents. Upon fine felt mats, you accord them the highest courtesy, probing the wellsprings of the heart through ancient teachings. Your concern reaches deep into the foundations of government, giving assurance of a reign enduring through generations, as divined for the house of Zhou. Your attentive hearing extends throughout the assembled official ranks, revealing a splendor like that of the Han emperor’s visit to the imperial academy.

The gold-adorned imperial carriage rolls like thunder; your arrival at the precious terrace is like the descent of a star. At the spacious seats and grand banquet, those present draw close to the pure serenity of the imperial countenance. The sumptuous dishes and mellow wine hold within them the fragrant richness of the supreme Way. translation_en:
…at Hao. Banners and standards shine with brilliant colors, inspiring outstanding men as they are summoned from every quarter; the zhi and jue notes sound in harmony, revealing the mutual delight of ruler and ministers. We reflect deeply that Your Majesty’s gracious regard is no mere adornment for outward show. Solemn are the commands proclaimed to the assembled court of Zhou; harmonious is the raising of cups in the elegant songs of Bin. The dignity of the scholarly officials is enhanced, and all officers rejoice in their nurture under Your Majesty’s influence. Your virtuous intentions silently win trust, and all the people eagerly devote themselves to the fundamental occupation of agriculture.

We, your servants, have long unworthily occupied the ranks of honored officials, and have all received generous marks of favor. The banquet is spread in the Jinhua Hall; invited to ascend, we step forward with reverent apprehension. The wine vessels brim with precious sweet wine; we withdraw from the meal at ease. Following antiquity in presenting these words, we feel deeply ashamed to fall short of the loyal counsel of seasoned elders. Bearing your kindness in our hearts, we compose this eulogy, hoping to join the people in their songs at leisure.

We humbly wish that, by nourishing the worthy, you may extend your bounty to all the people, while Heaven and Earth unite in harmony; and that, continuing the light, you may preside over the Nine Regions, while sun and moon remain steadfastly bright. Fragrant is the grain offering, sweet is the pepper’s scent: may all the rites of a plentiful year be fully observed. Inebriated with wine and sated with virtue, may you receive great blessings for ten thousand years. We, your servants, gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your Sagely Majesty, cannot contain our fervent emotion and utmost reverent trembling. We respectfully submit this memorial to express our thanks and make them known to you.

Third Session

Zheng Weicheng

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: This policy essay ably extols the excellence of our imperial ancestors in founding the dynasty and succeeding to its rule. It gives ample evidence of loyalty and devotion.

測贊揚者也盍嘗誦典謨而思君臣歌雅
頌而慕商周古之忠愛之臣務稱揚其君
之美凡以爲後王後賢告俾其習於耳浹
於心以無忘厥初也愚生雖不及此安敢
無有以就正乎天將弭非常之變則必授
之非常之才哉
聖祖不階尺土提三尺劍汛掃彌天之虜此豈
培塿勝爲憑資者耶然而鍾山龍蟠石頭
虎踞俯扼天塹自古以爲帝王之居南都
諸將亦嘗十取勝於江北金陵地勢豈可
少耶偏安之餘氣奪志衰其强易弱矣據
在人非地之罪也
聖祖嘗有意乎都大梁矣是以鳳陽爲中都也
氏勞甫定深慮而中止竊觀漢代秦唐代
隋宋代周皆即故地而居之元氏之都乃
爲
太宗封邑豈非天平中人之說起於周而西都
punctuated:
神謨以定不拔之業，皆非淺見陋聞所得而窺測贊揚者也。盖嘗誦典謨而思唐虞，歌雅頌而慕商周。古之忠愛之臣，務贊揚其君之美，凡以為後王後賢告，俾其習於耳，浹於心，以無忘厥初也。愚生雖不及此，安敢無言以就正乎？
天將弭非常之變，則必授之於非常之才。我聖祖不階尺土，提三尺劍，汛掃彌天之虜，此豈資形勝為憑資者耶？然而鍾山龍蟠，石頭虎踞，俯扼天塹，自古以為帝王之居。南朝諸將亦嘗十取勝於江北，金陵地勢豈可少耶？偏安之餘，氣奪志衰，其强易弱，夫據在人，非地之罪也。
聖祖嘗有意乎都大梁矣，是以鳳陽為中都也。民勞甫定，深慮而中止。竊觀漢代秦，唐代隋，宋代周，皆即故地而居之。元氏之都乃為太宗封邑，豈非天乎？中人之說起於周，而西都
translation_en:
…divine plans with which to establish an unshakable imperial enterprise: these are all beyond the ability of those of shallow insight and limited learning to fathom and extol. I have recited the Canons and Counsels and reflected upon Tang and Yu, sung the Odes and Eulogies and admired Shang and Zhou. The loyal and devoted ministers of antiquity strove to extol their rulers’ virtues, always intending thereby to instruct later kings and worthy men, so that these teachings would become familiar to their ears and permeate their hearts, and they would never forget the beginnings of their enterprise. Though I, an unworthy student, fall short of this, how could I dare remain silent rather than submit my words for correction?
When Heaven intends to quell extraordinary upheaval, it must entrust the task to a person of extraordinary ability. Our Sacred Founder rose without so much as a foot of territory and, wielding a three-foot sword, swept away the enemy who filled the world. Did he accomplish this by relying upon strategic advantages of terrain [?]? Nevertheless, Zhongshan coils like a dragon, and Shitou crouches like a tiger; overlooking and commanding the natural moat of the Yangzi, this site has been regarded since antiquity as a dwelling place for emperors and kings. The generals of the Southern Dynasties also won victories ten times north of the Yangzi. Can Jinling’s geographical advantages be belittled? After prolonged confinement to a regional domain, their spirit was broken and their resolve weakened; their strength turned to weakness. Holding a position depends upon people: the fault does not lie with the terrain.
The Sacred Founder once intended to establish his capital at Daliang; thus he made Fengyang the Central Capital. The people were exhausted and order had only just been restored, so after deep deliberation he abandoned the project. I humbly observe that when Han replaced Qin, Tang replaced Sui, and Song replaced Zhou, each settled in the former dynasty’s territory. The Yuan capital, however, became Taizong’s fief. Was this not Heaven’s doing? The idea of the ‘central person’ [?] originated in Zhou, yet the western capital…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
實在豐鎬堯舜吾□□□河拱□□□今
海達河今京師右太行左滄海背負醫無
閭囊括宇内盖自軒轅邑于涿鹿之阿及
今始再為畿甸不亦宜乎昔者秦人流毒
於民數百載漢高帝起布衣而代之湯武
夏商之建國也以獨夫之罪而遷其數百
年之統雖曰順天應人而名義所值漢實
為優我
聖祖收復五帝三王之中國本非元氏所宜有
===
殷周漢皆下風矣秦亂已極漢適承其敝
元氏承平百年失職之民方興思亂我
聖祖適當其難又誠不忍殘民踈欲徐觀天命
之集耳此孟子所以不敢望周文王也及
夫丁未之冬天戈北指則凡漢氏五年百
戰之區大將軍數月平定之矣豈以遲速
為優劣哉元承遼金而遼襲河北之亂巢
穴相因幾世幾年一旦空之蛟困涸溪虎
號中野豈一日忘故意哉

實在豐鎬堯舜□□□□□□□□
海逮河今京師右太行左滄海背□□□
閭囊括宇內盍自軒轅邑于涿鹿之阿及
今始西爲畿甸不亦宜乎昔者秦人流毒
於民數百載漢高帝起布衣而代之湯武
夏商之違國也以獨夫之罪而遷其數百
年之統雖曰順天應人而名義所值漢實
爲優我
聖祖肇修五帝三王之中國本非元氏所宜有
===
殷周漢皆下風矣秦亂已極漢適承其敝
元氏承平百年失職之民方興思亂我
聖祖適當艱難又誠不忍殘民棘欲徐觀天命
之集耳此孟子所以不敢望周文王也及
天下未之冬天戈北指則凡漢氏五年百
戰之區大將軍數月平定之矣豈以遲速
爲優劣哉元承遼金而遼襲河北之亂巢
穴相因幾世幾年一旦空之蛟困涸溪虎
號中野豈一日忘故意哉
punctuated: 實在豐鎬。堯舜吾□□□河拱□□□今海達河。今京師右太行，左滄海，背負醫無閭，囊括宇内。盖自軒轅邑于涿鹿之阿，及今始再為畿甸，不亦宜乎？昔者秦人流毒於民數百載，漢高帝起布衣而代之。湯武夏商之建國也，以獨夫之罪而遷其數百年之統，雖曰順天應人，而名義所值，漢實為優。我聖祖收復五帝三王之中國，本非元氏所宜有，殷周漢皆下風矣。秦亂已極，漢適承其敝；元氏承平百年，失職之民方興思亂，我聖祖適當其難，又誠不忍殘民，踈欲徐觀天命之集耳。此孟子所以不敢望周文王也。及夫丁未之冬，天戈北指，則凡漢氏五年百戰之區，大將軍數月平定之矣。豈以遲速為優劣哉？元承遼金，而遼襲河北之亂，巢穴相因，幾世幾年，一旦空之。蛟困涸溪，虎號中野，豈一日忘故意哉？
translation_en:
…was actually at Feng and Hao. Yao and Shun … [the transcription is illegible and garbled here; references to a river and the sea remain discernible][?]. The present capital has the Taihang Mountains on its right, the vast sea on its left, and Mount Yiwulü at its back; it embraces all within the realm. Since Xuanyuan established his settlement at the foot of Zhuolu, only now has this region again become the capital domain. Is this not fitting?

In former times, the people of Qin inflicted their poison upon the populace for several hundred years. Emperor Gao of Han rose from commoner status and supplanted them. As for Tang and Wu and the founding of states under Xia and Shang [?], they invoked the crimes of a solitary tyrant to transfer a dynastic succession that had endured for several hundred years. Although this was called following Heaven and responding to the people, in terms of the moral justification involved, Han was indeed superior. Our Sagely Progenitor recovered the central realm of the Five Emperors and Three Kings, which was never rightfully the possession of the Yuan house. Yin, Zhou, and Han all fall below him.

The disorder under Qin had already reached its extreme, and Han happened to inherit its exhausted condition. The Yuan house, however, had enjoyed a hundred years of peace; people deprived of their livelihoods were only beginning to stir and contemplate rebellion. Our Sagely Progenitor confronted precisely this difficulty. Moreover, he truly could not bear to bring suffering upon the people and wished [?] to observe at leisure where Heaven’s Mandate would gather. This is why Mencius did not dare hope to equal King Wen of Zhou.

When, in the winter of the dingwei year [1367], the heavenly weapons pointed north, the General-in-chief pacified in a few months all the territory over which Han had fought a hundred battles in five years. How could superiority or inferiority be judged by slowness or speed? Yuan succeeded Liao and Jin, while Liao had inherited the disorder in Hebei. Their lairs had been handed down through how many generations and years, only to be emptied in a single stroke. Like dragons trapped in a dried-up stream and tigers roaring in the open wilderness, could they forget their former ambitions for even a day?

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
太宗六飛三駕躬御戎馬暴露風沙不以耀兵
爲諱蓋爲中原千百世計耳武王滅國五
十成王猶不免四征不庭此召公所以進
張皇六師之戒於康王也漢三君之事姑
未論矣永樂己丑肇建北京置行在諸司
庚子定都于北備置諸司罷行在之稱而
以故都爲南京洪煕乙巳以後故都去南
京之號而北京復稱行在蓋皆委曲遷延
其間以聽人心之自定及夫正統辛酉始
===
復降南京府部諸印而京師定于北矣未
及十年而有己巳之變人心動摇卒協廟
廊之謀厎寧中外之難北辰奠極海宇會
歸是
四宗之勤而
景皇帝實成之者也夫以我
祖宗之創造如此其難而
列聖之所以恢弘而補苴之者如此其至
聖武之布昭固高出乎宇宙之上而

===
復降南京府部諸印而京師定于北矣未
及十年而有己巳之變人心動搖卒協廟
謨之謀底寧中外之難北辰奠極海宇會
歸是
四宗之勤而
景皇帝實成之者也夫以我
祖宗之創造如此其難而
列聖之所以恢弘而補葺之者如此其至
聖武之布昭固高出乎宇宙之上而
punctuated: 太宗六飛三駕，躬御戎馬，暴露風沙，不以耀兵爲諱，蓋爲中原千百世計耳。武王滅國五十，成王猶不免四征不庭，此召公所以進張皇六師之戒於康王也。漢三君之事，姑未論矣。永樂己丑，肇建北京，置行在諸司。庚子，定都于北，備置諸司，罷行在之稱，而以故都爲南京。洪煕乙巳以後，故都去南京之號，而北京復稱行在，蓋皆委曲遷延其間，以聽人心之自定。及夫正統辛酉，始復降南京府部諸印，而京師定于北矣。未及十年，而有己巳之變，人心動摇，卒協廟廊之謀，厎寧中外之難，北辰奠極，海宇會歸，是四宗之勤，而景皇帝實成之者也。夫以我祖宗之創造如此其難，而列聖之所以恢弘而補苴之者如此其至，聖武之布昭，固高出乎宇宙之上，而
translation_en:
Taizong’s six-steed imperial carriage set forth three times; he personally rode his warhorse, exposed to wind and sand, and did not shrink from displaying military might. His purpose was to provide for the Central Plain for a thousand, indeed ten thousand, generations. King Wu destroyed fifty states, yet King Cheng still could not avoid campaigning in all four directions against those who would not submit to his court. This was why the Duke of Shao admonished King Kang to expand and strengthen the Six Armies. Let us leave aside for now the affairs of the three Han rulers.

In the jichou year of Yongle (1409), construction of Beijing began, and offices were established there for the emperor’s temporary residence. In the gengzi year (1420), the capital was fixed in the north, the full complement of offices was established, and the designation “temporary imperial residence” was abolished, while the former capital became Nanjing. After the yisi year of Hongxi (1425), the former capital’s designation as Nanjing was removed, and Beijing was again called the temporary imperial residence. These were all measured accommodations and delays, allowing people’s sentiments to settle of themselves. Only in the xinyou year of Zhengtong (1441) were seals for Nanjing’s prefecture and ministries again issued, and the imperial capital became firmly established in the north.

Before ten years had passed, however, the crisis of the jisi year (1449) occurred, and people’s confidence wavered. In the end, through concerted plans at court, the troubles within and without were quelled. The Northern Pole Star was firmly established in its position, and all within the seas converged in allegiance. This was the labor of four ancestral emperors, but it was Emperor Jing who actually brought it to completion.

Considering how difficult the founding work of our imperial ancestors was, and how consummately their sagely successors enlarged it and remedied its deficiencies, the manifest brilliance of their sagely martial might assuredly towers above the universe, and…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
廟謨之深遠又默傳於宥密之中是宜威靈震
遠邇緒業垂無疆者也繹思求定亦豈在
多說乎哉念
王業之惟艱也則從而思曰櫛風沐雨以定
之俾我垂衣以治乎念民力之當重也則
從而思曰輸將大廣不可弛以與民乎念
定都之勿亟也則從而思曰舉大事可無
僉謀而緩圖乎念守成之不可忘武也則
從而思曰謀臣猛將可一日而不備乎念
猾夏之謀未殄也則從而思曰三陲防禦
可一日而不飭乎念南畿之為留都奧區
也則從而思曰根本重地可無以爲之封
殖乎念北畿之隣于邊也則從而思曰繭
絲保障其可並用以困民乎動無遺慮則
燕翼之謀可得而講也行無越思則仁民
之政可得而舉也有以光於前有以裕於
後則
休聲宏烈可得而嗣傳也如其不然則雖作

translation_en:
…the profound and far-reaching plans of the imperial court were also silently transmitted amid its secluded deliberations. It is fitting, therefore, that their awe-inspiring power should shake both far and near, and that their enduring achievements should be handed down without limit. In pondering these matters to reach settled conclusions, can much talk really be necessary?

When considering the hardships of establishing royal rule, one should then reflect: “They braved wind and rain to establish it, so that I might govern with my robes hanging loosely, at ease?” When considering how the people’s strength must be valued, one should then reflect: “Deliveries of supplies are exceedingly extensive; could these burdens not be eased to give relief to the people?” When considering that establishing the capital must not be rushed, one should then reflect: “Can a great undertaking proceed without consulting all concerned and planning deliberately?” When considering that preserving established rule requires remembering military preparedness, one should then reflect: “Can we go even a single day without having strategists and valiant generals ready?” When considering that designs to disturb China have not yet been extinguished, one should then reflect: “Can the defenses of the three frontiers go even a single day without being put in order?” When considering that the southern metropolitan region is the heartland surrounding the secondary capital, one should then reflect: “Can this vital foundation of the realm be left without measures to nurture and strengthen it?” When considering that the northern metropolitan region adjoins the frontier, one should then reflect: “Can the extraction of revenue and the provision of defense both be imposed so as to exhaust the people?”

If no consideration is overlooked when taking action, plans to provide security for descendants can be discussed. If conduct never outruns reflection, policies that care benevolently for the people can be implemented. With means to bring glory to those who came before and leave abundance to those who follow, their splendid reputation and great achievements can be carried on and transmitted. If this is not so, then even if one produces…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
張揚厲瑰偉鏗鏘以美觀聽則有之於治
道奚益哉是則愚生之所不敢聞也
第二問
鄭莊彦
同考試官教諭王批人才一策正欲觀
士子博古之學心術之辨作者殊無定見此作
心術正大品第允當用録以式
同考試官教諭顏批義利王霸乃古人
心迹異處子能言之可以占所趨矣
===
同考試官教諭王批策體大而蓄辭博
而雅氣實而充有根據有斷制有抑揚雖數賢
輩復出亦當面服其議子之蘊積可知矣
考試官左賛善張批内外合一之謂道子
能於古人心術功業異同處而斷之以道他日
致用知必不謬於所趨矣
考試官右諭德倫批商畧終古人才非胸
中銖兩素定者不能也吾子其可與言已夫
知義利之分可與語道矣知王霸之辨可

張揚厲，瑰偉鏗鏘，以美觀聽則有之，於治道奚益哉？是則愚生之所不敢聞也。
第二問
鄭莊彦

…grandiloquent display, magnificent and sonorous, may indeed delight the eye and ear; but what benefit does it bring to the way of governing? This is something that I, an unworthy student, would not presume to entertain.
Second Question
Zheng Zhuangyan
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: This policy question on men of talent was intended precisely to reveal the candidates’ breadth of learning about antiquity and their discernment concerning motives and moral dispositions. The writers generally lacked settled judgments. This essay shows an upright and magnanimous moral disposition, and its assessments are fair and appropriate. It is therefore selected for inclusion as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yan, Instructor: Righteousness and profit, and the ways of the true king and the hegemon, mark the differences in the intentions and actions of men of antiquity. Your ability to discuss these allows us to discern the direction of your own aspirations.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: The policy essay is broad in scope and rich in substance; its language is ample and elegant, its vitality substantial and abundant. It has solid grounding, decisive judgments, and due praise and criticism. Even if those worthy men were to return to life, they would have to acknowledge its arguments to your face. The depth of your accumulated learning is evident.

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
與語用矣知得失之理可與語政矣知盛
衰之端可與語天矣知治亂之機可與語
時矣故其道得者其用備其政一其端實
其機張其道失者其用偏其政二其端虛
其機弛故道其本也用其紀也政其實也
端其微也機其成也君子道以為經用以
為則政以為質端以為量機以為符道以
為經故其本可立也用以為則故其紀可
興也政以為質故其實可守也端以為量
===
故其微可測也機以為符故其成可睹也
是以君子欲正天下不知其機不能正天
下知其機不知其端不能正天下知其端
不知其政不能正天下知其政不知其用
不能正天下知其用不知其道不能正天
下故道者理萬物達天道順人情之大端
也故惟君子為知道之不可以已也至道
之世渾渾爾噩噩爾其政悶悶其民醇醇
君臣相忘合天履中道貫萬化不言而信

translation_en: …one may discuss practical application with him. With one who understands the principles of success and failure, one may discuss government. With one who understands the beginnings of flourishing and decline, one may discuss Heaven. With one who understands the pivotal workings of order and disorder, one may discuss the times. Thus, when the Way is attained, its application is complete, government is unified, its beginnings are substantial, and its pivotal workings are activated. When the Way is lost, its application is partial, government is divided, its beginnings are empty, and its pivotal workings slacken. The Way is the root; application is the organizing framework; government is the substance; beginnings are the subtle indications; and pivotal workings bring fulfillment. The gentleman takes the Way as his guiding thread, application as his rule, government as his substance, beginnings as his measure, and pivotal workings as his verifying token. Taking the Way as his guiding thread, he can establish the root; taking application as his rule, he can set the organizing framework in motion; taking government as his substance, he can preserve what is substantial; taking beginnings as his measure, he can discern the subtle indications; taking pivotal workings as his verifying token, he can see the fulfillment. Thus, if the gentleman wishes to set the world right but does not understand its pivotal workings, he cannot do so. If he understands its pivotal workings but not its beginnings, he cannot set the world right. If he understands its beginnings but not its government, he cannot set the world right. If he understands its government but not its practical application, he cannot set the world right. If he understands its practical application but not its Way, he cannot set the world right. The Way is therefore the great foundation for ordering all things, comprehending the Way of Heaven, and following human feelings. Thus, only the gentleman understands that pursuit of the Way must never cease. In an age of the highest Way, all is simple and uncontrived; government is unobtrusive, and the people are sincere and pure. Ruler and ministers forget the distinctions between them, accord with Heaven, and tread the mean. The Way pervades all transformations, and trust prevails without words…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
不辨而理生民宜焉萬物順焉如天地平
所勞於物而物各得其性物雖各得其性
而不知其爲天地之功也不知其功孰爲
其端不知其天孰爲其機哉及其季也義
不勝其利而道之本喪矣王不勝其霸而
用之紀偏矣得不勝其失而政之實亡矣
盛不勝其衰而端之微虛矣治不勝其亂
而機之成弛矣不反其原而乃咎其流之
滔滔也亦惑哉三代之得天下也以仁其
===
失天下也以不仁仁不仁人實爲之也於
天何尤乎故曰知盛衰之端可與語天矣
知治亂之機可與語時矣春秋之世臣弑
其君子弑其父非一朝一夕之故也所賴
以撥亂而反之正者獨存乎君子爾然不
能使春秋之不爲春秋者愚於當時數子
則不能無憾焉齊之賢莫鮑叔管仲也晉
之賢莫舅犯趙衰先軫郤克也宋之賢莫
華元也楚之賢莫子文蔿賈也秦之賢莫

punctuated:
不辨而理，生民宜焉，萬物順焉。如天地平所勞於物，而物各得其性；物雖各得其性，而不知其爲天地之功也。不知其功，孰爲其端？不知其天，孰爲其機哉？及其季也，義不勝其利，而道之本喪矣；王不勝其霸，而用之紀偏矣；得不勝其失，而政之實亡矣；盛不勝其衰，而端之微虛矣；治不勝其亂，而機之成弛矣。不反其原，而乃咎其流之滔滔也，亦惑哉！三代之得天下也以仁，其失天下也以不仁。仁不仁，人實爲之也，於天何尤乎？故曰：「知盛衰之端，可與語天矣；知治亂之機，可與語時矣。」

春秋之世，臣弑其君，子弑其父，非一朝一夕之故也。所賴以撥亂而反之正者，獨存乎君子爾。然不能使春秋之不爲春秋者，愚於當時數子則不能無憾焉。齊之賢莫鮑叔、管仲也；晉之賢莫舅犯、趙衰、先軫、郤克也；宋之賢莫華元也；楚之賢莫子文、蔿賈也；秦之賢莫
translation_en:
…order prevails without disputation; the people find their proper condition, and all things follow their proper course. It is like Heaven and Earth, which expend no effort upon things [?], yet each thing realizes its own nature. Although each realizes its own nature, none knows that this is the achievement of Heaven and Earth. If their achievement is unknown, who can identify its beginnings? If Heaven is unknown, who can identify its pivotal workings? When an age reaches its decline, righteousness cannot prevail over profit, and the foundation of the Way is lost; kingly rule cannot prevail over hegemonic rule, and the guiding principles of practical action become distorted; gains cannot prevail over losses, and the substance of government disappears; flourishing cannot prevail over decline, and the subtle beginnings lose their substance; order cannot prevail over disorder, and the workings that bring things to fruition slacken. To fail to return to the source, yet blame the rushing torrent downstream—is this not delusion? The Three Dynasties gained All-under-Heaven through benevolence and lost it through lack of benevolence. Benevolence and its absence are indeed the work of human beings: what grounds are there for blaming Heaven? Thus it is said: “With one who understands the beginnings of flourishing and decline, one may discuss Heaven; with one who understands the pivotal workings of order and disorder, one may discuss the times.”

In the Spring and Autumn period, ministers murdered their rulers and sons murdered their fathers. These developments did not arise in a single morning or evening. Those upon whom one could rely to quell disorder and restore what was right were solely the gentlemen. Yet they could not prevent the Spring and Autumn age from being what it was; in my humble view, I cannot but feel regret concerning those few men of that time. Among the worthy men of Qi, none surpassed Bao Shu and Guan Zhong; among those of Jin, none surpassed Jiu Fan, Zhao Cui, Xian Zhen, and Xi Ke; among those of Song, none surpassed Hua Yuan; among those of Chu, none surpassed Ziwen and Wei Jia; among those of Qin, none surpassed…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
百里奚也鄭之賢莫子產也吳之賢莫季
札也然夷攷其事曰翊謀定國知人則多
也曰九合諸侯一匡天下也曰賛定王室
宣信諸侯也曰深智逺謀也曰報施定覇
也曰伐齊威眾也曰執詞却敵宣力靖難
也曰治兵之善楚以浸强也曰料事之識
幼而克哲也曰知先虞亡猷克秦乂也曰
善辭振國平政惠民也曰慕義見微閱覽
博物也而聖賢脩身治人之道初不之講
焉故以管仲之仁猶不免器小之病以季
札之賢尚不明達節之權二子且然其餘
尚何足論哉朱子曰五覇竊仁義之號以
令諸侯使有王者作而以仁義之實施之
則爝火之光其息久矣是也許氏謂春秋
氣運之厄有以成吾道之厄殆亦未盡之
論歟漢興去古未逺而高帝開之以寬仁
唐則戡隋之亂而太宗行之以仁義此興
治之一機矣所望以翊亮元化以復先王

百里奚也；鄭之賢莫子產也；吳之賢莫季札也。然夷攷其事，曰翊謀定國，知人則多也；曰九合諸侯，一匡天下也；曰賛定王室，宣信諸侯也；曰深智逺謀也；曰報施定覇也；曰伐齊威眾也；曰執詞却敵，宣力靖難也；曰治兵之善，楚以浸强也；曰料事之識，幼而克哲也；曰知先虞亡，猷克秦乂也；曰善辭振國，平政惠民也；曰慕義見微，閱覽博物也。而聖賢脩身治人之道，初不之講焉。故以管仲之仁，猶不免器小之病；以季札之賢，尚不明達節之權。二子且然，其餘尚何足論哉！朱子曰：「五覇竊仁義之號以令諸侯，使有王者作而以仁義之實施之，則爝火之光其息久矣。」是也。許氏謂春秋氣運之厄，有以成吾道之厄，殆亦未盡之論歟！

translation_en:
…Baili Xi; among the worthy men of Zheng, none surpassed Zichan; among those of Wu, none surpassed Jizha. Yet, examining their deeds impartially, what can be said of them is this: one assisted in planning and secured the state, with considerable discernment of men; another assembled the feudal lords nine times and set all under Heaven right; another helped stabilize the royal house and made his good faith known among the feudal lords; another possessed profound wisdom and foresight; another repaid favors and established hegemony; another attacked Qi and overawed the multitude; another wielded arguments to repel enemies and exerted himself to quell disorders; another managed armies so well that Chu gradually grew strong; another showed discernment in judging affairs and was wise even in youth; another foresaw Yu’s downfall and devised plans that brought Qin good government [?]; another excelled in diplomatic speech, reinvigorated his state, made government equitable, and benefited the people; another admired righteousness, perceived subtle signs, and acquired extensive knowledge through his observations. Yet they never studied the sages’ and worthies’ Way of cultivating oneself and governing others. Thus even Guan Zhong, for all his benevolence, could not escape the failing of limited capacity; even Jizha, for all his worthiness, did not understand the discretionary judgment needed to adapt moral principles to circumstances. If even these two were like this, how could the others merit further discussion? Master Zhu said: “The Five Hegemons appropriated the names of benevolence and righteousness to command the feudal lords. Had a true king arisen and put the substance of benevolence and righteousness into practice, their torchlight would long since have been extinguished.” This is correct. Master Xu’s claim that the adversity of the age’s cosmic fortunes in the Spring and Autumn period helped bring adversity upon our Way is perhaps also an account that does not go far enough!

When the Han arose, antiquity was not yet far distant, and Emperor Gao inaugurated it with generosity and benevolence. The Tang quelled the disorders of the Sui, and Emperor Taizong governed through benevolence and righteousness. These were opportunities for bringing good government into being. Those upon whom rested the hope of assisting the sovereign’s transforming influence and restoring the former kings’…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之政者則存乎輔弼耳然其治卒不免於
雜覇雜夷者愚於當時諸人則不能無恨
焉漢之賢莫蕭何曹參也莫丙吉魏相也
唐之賢莫房玄齡杜如晦也莫姚崇宋璟
也然夷攷其事曰與民更始講若畫一也
曰市獄勿擾清淨不事也曰深厚不伐不
親小事也曰條奏便宜數稱上意也曰明
達吏事也曰遇事善决也曰應變成務也
曰守法持正也而大人格心之學初未之
===
聞焉故蕭何以沛邑故人不能定天下之
本魏相以嚴明相濟不能抑許史之權推
刃同氣至慘矣何取於謀寵移婦寺至惑
矣何取於正其大如此其小者又何足言
哉朱子曰後來英雄未嘗有精一工夫但
在利欲場中頭出頭沒其資美者乃能有
所暗合而隨其分數之多少以有所建立
者是也許氏謂春秋人才雖非王者之佐
而皆漢唐所不能及者其或有見之言歟

punctuated: 之政者，則存乎輔弼耳。然其治卒不免於雜覇雜夷者，愚於當時諸人則不能無恨焉。漢之賢，莫蕭何、曹參也，莫丙吉、魏相也；唐之賢，莫房玄齡、杜如晦也，莫姚崇、宋璟也。然夷攷其事，曰與民更始，講若畫一也；曰市獄勿擾，清淨不事也；曰深厚不伐，不親小事也；曰條奏便宜，數稱上意也；曰明達吏事也；曰遇事善决也；曰應變成務也；曰守法持正也。而大人格心之學，初未之聞焉。故蕭何以沛邑故人，不能定天下之本；魏相以嚴明相濟，不能抑許史之權。推刃同氣，至慘矣，何取於謀？寵移婦寺，至惑矣，何取於正？其大如此，其小者又何足言哉！朱子曰：「後來英雄，未嘗有精一工夫，但在利欲場中頭出頭沒，其資美者乃能有所暗合，而隨其分數之多少以有所建立者。」是也。許氏謂春秋人才雖非王者之佐，而皆漢唐所不能及者，其或有見之言歟？
translation_en:
…the government of the former kings depended upon the ministers who assisted the ruler. Yet their rule ultimately remained mixed with hegemonic and barbarian practices; I cannot but feel regret over the men of those times. Among the worthy men of the Han, none surpassed Xiao He and Cao Can, or Bing Ji and Wei Xiang; among those of the Tang, none surpassed Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui, or Yao Chong and Song Jing. Yet, examining their deeds impartially, we find these descriptions: making a fresh beginning with the people and establishing uniform rules [?]; leaving markets and prisons undisturbed, maintaining tranquillity and avoiding intervention; being profound and generous without boasting, and not personally attending to minor matters; submitting itemized proposals for expedient measures and frequently satisfying the emperor’s wishes; understanding administrative affairs clearly; deciding matters skilfully as they arose; responding to changing circumstances and accomplishing tasks; and upholding the law and maintaining rectitude. But of the great man’s learning, which rectifies the ruler’s heart, we hear nothing at all.

Thus Xiao He, though an old acquaintance from Pei, could not secure the foundation of the realm; Wei Xiang, though combining strictness with discernment, could not curb the power of the Xu and Shi families. Turning the blade against one’s own brothers was cruelty in the extreme: what merit was there in such counsel? Imperial favor shifting to women and eunuchs was delusion in the extreme: what merit was there in such rectitude? If their conduct in great matters was like this, what need is there to discuss the lesser ones?

Master Zhu said: “The heroic men of later ages never undertook the work of refinement and singleness of purpose. They merely bobbed up and down in the arena of profit and desire. Those endowed with fine qualities could achieve some unwitting accord with the Way, and establish accomplishments in proportion to the measure of that accord.” This is indeed so. Master Xu maintained that, although the talented men of the Spring and Autumn period were not helpers of true kings, they were all beyond the reach of the men of the Han and Tang. Might these words contain some insight?

text:
至若孔子生乎春秋之世其却萊夷堕三
都誅少正卯駸駸乎帝王之業使能久於
位如數子焉則吾其東周豈虛語哉孟子
丁乎戰國之時其仁義之言性善之說井
田之對鑿鑿乎王道之大使得措之行如
數子焉則齊王反手豈欺我哉道既不行
則退而托之著述以教萬世雖不能挽春
秋戰國而唐虞三代也然使唐虞三代之
人心不盡亡於春秋戰國者則孔孟之功
===

者之心使君臣父子之倫不盡壞於盜賊

text:
躬盡瘁雖不幸中道而殞然其扶皇極正
人心挽回先王仁義之風垂之萬世與日
月同其光明楊中立曰狄梁公撥亂反正
然亦何嘗挾數任術觀史氏所載其議論
未嘗不以正其深知二子者哉夫春秋數
子處其順而孔孟處其逆漢唐諸人處其
常而武侯梁公處其變順逆常變之間而
事之難易心之是非君子可以槩見也故
曰知義利之分可與語道矣知王霸之辨
===
可與語用矣雖然塗有餓莩而五穀無全
功元氣潰决而參苓無全力然君子終不
以荑稗易五穀以烏喙易參苓者誠以荑
稗非養生之具而烏喙之烈不可常試也
夫義譬則五穀也利譬則荑稗也王譬則
參苓也霸譬則烏喙也人徒見夫荑稗之
易成而烏喙之得乎近效也遂從而嗜之
不厭而不知其身之元氣已索然而不可
起矣人見其索然而不可起也則諉曰是

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
歲也命也豈非愚之甚哉或者曰天下之
事有幸不幸其理之是者或屈於勢之難
而理之非者或徇於勢之易故君子每不
得其常焉噫事勢無一定之形而道則不
可易焉者也如道焉勢雖難君子弗避也
非道焉勢雖易君子弗爲也苟枉其道以
幸必成之功則一時雖甚快而禍之貽於
天下者必多矣愚又悲夫世之爲義者鮮
不爲利而爲之也夫爲利者人皆知其爲
===
小人也而爲利以爲義者彼方侈然自是
而舉世譽以爲功不知其爲害於國家之
深也故曰知得失之理可與語政矣狂瞽
之言不知所裁惟執事進而教之
第三問
同考試官訓導王批治道一策正欲探
士子用世之蘊是作援推古今言有體要高薦
夫何疑

得其常焉噫事勢無一定之形而道則不
可易焉者也如道焉勢雖難君子弗避也
非道焉勢雖易君子弗為也茍枉其道以

小人也而為利以為義者彼方修然自是
而舉世譽以為功不知其為害於國家之
深也故曰知得失之理可與語政矣狂瞽

第三問
同考試官訓導王　批　治道一策正欲探
士子用世之藴是作論推古今言有體要高薦
夫何疑
punctuated:
歲也，命也。豈非愚之甚哉？或者曰：「天下之事有幸不幸，其理之是者或屈於勢之難，而理之非者或徇於勢之易，故君子每不得其常焉。」噫！事勢無一定之形，而道則不可易焉者也。如道焉，勢雖難，君子弗避也；非道焉，勢雖易，君子弗爲也。苟枉其道以幸必成之功，則一時雖甚快，而禍之貽於天下者必多矣。愚又悲夫世之爲義者，鮮不爲利而爲之也。夫爲利者，人皆知其爲小人也；而爲利以爲義者，彼方侈然自是，而舉世譽以爲功，不知其爲害於國家之深也。故曰：「知得失之理，可與語政矣。」狂瞽之言，不知所裁，惟執事進而教之。

第三問

同考試官訓導王批：「治道一策，正欲探士子用世之蘊。是作援推古今，言有體要。高薦，夫何疑？」
translation_en:
…the year’s conditions, or fate. Is this not the height of folly? Someone may say: “In the affairs of the world, there is good fortune and bad. What is right in principle may be thwarted by difficult circumstances, while what is wrong in principle may follow the ease afforded by circumstances. Thus the gentleman often cannot attain the normal outcome.” Alas! Circumstances have no fixed form, but the Way cannot be changed. If something accords with the Way, the gentleman does not shrink from it, however difficult the circumstances; if it departs from the Way, he will not undertake it, however easy the circumstances. If one bends the Way in the hope of securing certain success, the immediate gratification may be great, but the calamities bequeathed to the world will surely be many.

I grieve, moreover, that among those in this world who practice righteousness, few do so without seeking profit. Everyone recognizes those who pursue profit as petty men. Yet those who pursue profit under the guise of righteousness complacently consider themselves right, while the whole world praises their achievements, unaware of the profound harm they do to the state. Thus it is said: “With one who understands the principles of gain and loss, one may discuss government.” These are rash and unenlightened words; I do not know how to judge them. I ask only that you, sir, receive me and instruct me.

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭林批人臣進言必欲感
悟以底于行忠君之心也此策委曲於聽言之
喻且撮四子之要以備采擇子之心可識矣
考試官左贊善張批帝王之道不外乎此
心而已子能於四子之言而揭其至要以著于
篇則他日成格君之功者非子也耶
考試官右諭德倫批庶幾言近而指遠者
人君之興道致治其於古訓必有所稽也
人君之稽于古訓也其於心必有以自得
===
也人求多聞時惟建事學于古訓乃有獲
夫非心得焉惡能推而行之以為建事之
本哉夫苟有得于心則雖詢于芻蕘察于
邇言固吾益也而况古訓乎况古訓之出
于儒先賢聖者乎如其不然日取三王五
帝之典謨而左右陳說之豈能有濟哉昔
者劉元城問學於溫公而聞不妄語之教
非異人見也而元城之得益在是則必有
會于其心者矣雖然温公參問晚於蘇公而聞

考試官右諭德倫批：「庶幾言近而指遠者。」

人君之興道致治，其於古訓必有所稽也。人君之稽于古訓也，其於心必有以自得也。「人求多聞，時惟建事；學于古訓，乃有獲。」夫非心得焉，惡能推而行之，以為建事之本哉？夫苟有得于心，則雖詢于芻蕘、察于邇言，固吾益也，而况古訓乎？况古訓之出于儒先賢聖者乎？如其不然，日取三王五帝之典謨而左右陳說之，豈能有濟哉？昔者劉元城問學於溫公，而聞不妄語之教，非異人見也，而元城之得益在是，則必有會于其心者矣。雖然，温公參問晚於蘇公，而聞
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: “When a minister offers counsel, he necessarily hopes to awaken his ruler’s understanding and thereby bring him to act: this expresses loyalty to his sovereign. This policy essay explains with care and subtlety how counsel should be heard, and also draws together the essentials of the four masters’ teachings for consideration and selection. Your intentions can thus be understood.”

Examiner Zhang, Left Mentor, comments: “The Way of emperors and kings lies nowhere beyond this mind. From the words of the four masters, you have brought out what is most essential and set it forth in your essay. Will it not be you who one day succeeds in rectifying the ruler?”

Examiner Lun, Right Admonisher, comments: “This comes close to speaking in familiar terms while conveying a far-reaching meaning.”

For a ruler to promote the Way and bring about good government, he must consult the teachings of antiquity. In consulting those teachings, he must attain an understanding of his own within his mind. ‘When a person seeks extensive learning, it is for accomplishing affairs; by studying ancient teachings, one gains understanding.’ Unless he grasps them in his mind, how can he extend them into practice and make them the foundation for accomplishing affairs? If he has indeed gained an inward understanding, then even consulting grass-cutters and wood-gatherers and examining everyday sayings will assuredly benefit him. How much more so the teachings of antiquity! And how much more those ancient teachings that come from the sages and worthies among our Confucian predecessors! Otherwise, even if he daily takes up the canons and counsels of the Three Kings and Five Emperors and has them expounded on every side, how could this be of any help?

Formerly, Liu Yuancheng sought instruction from the Duke of Wen and heard his teaching against speaking falsely. This was no insight unfamiliar to others, yet Yuancheng benefited from it: it must therefore have struck home in his mind. Nevertheless, the Duke of Wen’s inquiries came later than those of the Duke of Su [?], and he heard …

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
清淨自定之教非異人見也而參之得益
在是則亦必有會于其心而然也人至于
今以温公為善教以蓋公為善言何則以
夫聽言者擇善之有術而亮乎其心之所
安也夫惟亮乎其心之所安則其信之必
深赴之必勇守之必固而授之言者不為
徒說矣夫以賓友之間而言之不可取必
也如是况夫人臣之進言于其君者哉人
臣進言於君盖莫敢不自盡焉而况將以
===
帝王之道致主者則其竭底裏效衷赤宜
何如也然其言之用與不用盖有數存焉
言之而是也用之為天下福言之而非也
用之為天下禍人臣進言豈徒不用之為
戚耶漢之武帝宣帝皆有帝王之才而董
仲舒王吉皆有致君之志者也武帝方事
夷狄求神仙欲敗度縱敗禮不可枚舉而
宣帝正武帝之流亞耳二子之說惡能用
之宋之神宗刻意王道而程子因以啓告

translation_en:
…the teaching that through purity and quietude things settle themselves was no extraordinary insight. Yet Can benefited from precisely this, so it must likewise have been because something in it resonated with his heart. To this day, people regard Lord Wen as skilled in teaching and Master Gai as skilled in counsel. Why? Because those who heard their words knew how to choose what was good and clearly understood what their own hearts found right. Only with this clarity would their conviction necessarily be deep, their pursuit resolute, and their adherence firm; then the words imparted to them would not be mere empty talk. Even among guests and friends, acceptance of counsel cannot be assured: how much more is this so when a minister offers counsel to his ruler? When ministers advise their ruler, surely none dares to withhold his utmost effort. How much more, then, should those who intend to guide their sovereign by the Way of the ancient emperors and kings lay bare their innermost thoughts and demonstrate their wholehearted sincerity!

Yet whether their words are adopted or rejected is subject to an allotted fate. If their counsel is right, adopting it brings blessings to all under Heaven; if it is wrong, adopting it brings calamity to all under Heaven. Should ministers who offer counsel grieve only that it is not adopted? Emperors Wu and Xuan of the Han both possessed the abilities of an emperor or king, while Dong Zhongshu and Wang Ji both aspired to lead their rulers to that ideal. Emperor Wu was then occupied with campaigns against the Yi and Di peoples and the pursuit of immortals; his desires undermined established standards, and his indulgence undermined ritual propriety, in instances too numerous to enumerate. Emperor Xuan was merely another of Emperor Wu’s kind. How could the counsel of these two men have been put into practice? Emperor Shenzong of the Song devoted himself earnestly to the Kingly Way, and Master Cheng accordingly offered him instruction…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
焉且自藝祖以來世濟仁厚邵子有感於
百年勝殘之運深有望于繼世之君豈知
神宗信任失人祖宗之澤頓熄而後此亦
無可爲之時矣一子之說又惡能用之此
無他不得乎其心言雖善無益也洪惟
昭代當重熙累洽之時仰值我
皇上赫然中興思濟大業百辟承德海內嚮風
所以賛襄萬一者詎謂無四子其人乎而
何俟乎草茅之贅論乎無已則愚姑繹四
===
子之言以備執事者之采擇也盖董子之
言曰正心以正朝廷正朝廷以正百官正
百官以正萬民正萬民以正四方吉之言
曰聖主獨行於深宫得則天下稱誦之失
則天下咸言之故謹選左右慎擇所使左
右所以正身也所使所以宣德也夫正心
慎獨之說自曾子子思之後知講之者鮮
矣而二子能言之其所謂加王心舉明主
於三代之隆者氏以是爲之根柢也豈非

所以贊襄萬一者詎謂無四子其人乎而

矣而二子能言之其所謂加王心舉明主
於三代之隆者凡以是爲之根柢也豈非
punctuated:
焉。且自藝祖以來，世濟仁厚。邵子有感於百年勝殘之運，深有望于繼世之君。豈知神宗信任失人，祖宗之澤頓熄，而後此亦無可爲之時矣！一子之說又惡能用之？此無他，不得乎其心，言雖善，無益也。
洪惟昭代，當重熙累洽之時，仰值我皇上赫然中興，思濟大業，百辟承德，海內嚮風。所以賛襄萬一者，詎謂無四子其人乎？而何俟乎草茅之贅論乎？無已，則愚姑繹四子之言，以備執事者之采擇也。
盖董子之言曰：「正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民，正萬民以正四方。」吉之言曰：「聖主獨行於深宫，得則天下稱誦之，失則天下咸言之。故謹選左右，慎擇所使。左右所以正身也，所使所以宣德也。」夫正心慎獨之說，自曾子、子思之後，知講之者鮮矣，而二子能言之。其所謂加王心、舉明主於三代之隆者，氏以是爲之根柢也。豈非
translation_en:
…to him. Moreover, from the time of the founding emperor, successive generations had sustained benevolence and generosity. Master Shao, moved by the prospect of overcoming cruelty after a hundred years of good government, placed great hopes in the succeeding ruler. Who could have known that Shenzong would place his trust in the wrong man, abruptly extinguishing the beneficent legacy of his ancestors, and that thereafter there would be no opportunity to accomplish anything? How, then, could this one master's teachings have been put into practice? The reason was simply that he had not won the ruler's heart: however good his words, they were of no avail.
Reflecting reverently upon our illustrious dynasty, in this age of accumulated splendor and enduring peace, we are privileged to live under our emperor, who has gloriously brought about a restoration and seeks to fulfill his great undertaking. The assembled officials uphold his virtue, and all within the seas turn toward his transforming influence. Among those who assist him even in the smallest measure, could it be said that there are none comparable to these four masters? Why, then, should there be any need for the superfluous discussion of an obscure commoner? Yet, if I must speak, I shall venture to expound the words of the four masters for you, the officials in charge, to consider and select from.
Master Dong said: “Rectify the heart in order to rectify the court; rectify the court in order to rectify the hundred officials; rectify the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people; rectify the myriad people in order to rectify the four quarters.” Wang Ji said: “When a sage ruler acts alone in the depths of the palace, if he acts rightly, all under Heaven praise him; if he errs, all under Heaven speak of it. Therefore, he carefully selects his attendants and cautiously chooses those whom he commissions. His attendants serve to rectify his person; those whom he commissions serve to spread his virtue.” Since Zengzi and Zisi, few have understood how to discuss the teachings of rectifying the heart and being watchful over oneself when alone, yet these two masters could articulate them. What they called bringing influence to bear upon the king's heart [?] and raising an enlightened ruler to the heights of the Three Dynasties took these teachings as its foundation [?]. Were they not …

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
西京諸儒之卓然有見者乎程子論行王
道以定志爲本君志定而天下之治成矣
必以聖賢之訓爲先當從以先王之治爲
必可法不爲後世駁雜之政所牽滯不爲
流俗因循之論所遷改信道極於篤自知
極於明去邪勿疑任賢勿貳此定志之說
雖聖人復起不能易也邵子之於帝道蓋
未嘗言之而其所恒言則曰天下將亂則
人必尚言也天下將治則人必尚行也尚
===
行則篤實之風行焉尚言則詭譎之風行
焉推是言也詭譎之流則覇圖之下衰也
篤實之崇則王治之上隆也教化浹而人
情變於是乎三變而帝道可舉使有聖人
繼世而興焉安知其言之不遂有徵乎道
不行百世無善治學不傳千載無真儒世
之論者必以爲帝王之治有卓絕殊尤之
跡而商帝王之畧者亦必有幽深玄遠之
論噫惑也久矣孔子答顏淵爲邦之間終

punctuated: 西京諸儒之卓然有見者乎？程子論行王道，以定志爲本，君志定而天下之治成矣。必以聖賢之訓爲先當從，以先王之治爲必可法，不爲後世駁雜之政所牽滯，不爲流俗因循之論所遷改，信道極於篤，自知極於明，去邪勿疑，任賢勿貳。此定志之說，雖聖人復起，不能易也。邵子之於帝道，蓋未嘗言之，而其所恒言則曰：「天下將亂，則人必尚言也；天下將治，則人必尚行也。尚行則篤實之風行焉，尚言則詭譎之風行焉。」推是言也，詭譎之流，則覇圖之下衰也；篤實之崇，則王治之上隆也。教化浹而人情變，於是乎三變而帝道可舉。使有聖人繼世而興焉，安知其言之不遂有徵乎？道不行，百世無善治；學不傳，千載無真儒。世之論者必以爲帝王之治有卓絕殊尤之跡，而商帝王之畧者亦必有幽深玄遠之論。噫！惑也久矣！孔子答顏淵爲邦之間，終
translation_en:
…those among the scholars of the Western Han who possessed outstanding insight? Master Cheng, discussing the practice of the kingly Way, took firmness of purpose as its foundation: once the ruler’s purpose is settled, orderly government throughout the realm can be achieved. One must regard the teachings of the sages and worthies as what should be followed first, and the government of the former kings as certainly worthy of emulation. One must neither be constrained by the mixed and impure policies of later ages nor be swayed by conventional arguments for following established habits. Faith in the Way must be utterly steadfast, and self-knowledge utterly clear. Remove the wicked without hesitation; employ the worthy without wavering. Even if a sage arose again, he could not alter this teaching on firmness of purpose.

As for the Way of the ancient emperors, Master Shao seems never to have spoken of it directly. What he repeatedly said was: “When the realm is about to fall into disorder, people invariably esteem talk; when the realm is about to become well governed, people invariably esteem action. When action is esteemed, a spirit of sincerity and substance prevails; when talk is esteemed, a spirit of deceit and cunning prevails.” Extending this saying’s implications, the spread of deceit and cunning marks the downward decline of hegemonic enterprise; the elevation of sincerity and substance marks the upward flourishing of kingly government. When moral instruction permeates society and people’s dispositions change, three transformations can then bring the Way of the ancient emperors into practice. If a sage were to arise in a succeeding age, how can we know that these words would not ultimately be borne out?

If the Way is not practiced, a hundred generations will have no good government; if learning is not transmitted, a thousand years will have no true Confucian scholars. Those who discuss such matters nowadays invariably suppose that the government of the ancient emperors and kings must display extraordinary and exceptional achievements, and that those who deliberate upon their governing methods must likewise offer abstruse and far-reaching arguments. Alas! How long this delusion has persisted! When Confucius answered Yan Yuan’s question [?] about governing a state, he concluded …

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之以放鄭聲遠佞人孟子勸齊梁之君以
行王道惟制民恒產是急自今視之皆以
為迂且淺而不知道固如是也然則四子
之言有能舉而措之其可勝用乎約而言
之取諸邵子則尚行其要也取諸程子則
定志其要也取諸西京二子則謹獨正心
其要也苟有會于吾心吾擇善而從之夫
庸知四子者學之純駁與其見之淺深耶
彼固有不量其君不察其時而强聒以進
===
者彼其遺恨於當時固將有望于百千載
之後耳若其條件節目之詳施為緩急之
序則所謂正其本萬事理未容以遽及也
擇言之道其博而取之如千蹊萬徑皆可
適國並存而無廢焉其約而會之如庖丁
解牛得其族則衆觧理矣不然吾未見其
為學古訓而有獲也漢申公有言為治者
不在多言顧力行何如耳請以是言終四
子之志執事以為何如

punctuated:
之以放鄭聲、遠佞人。孟子勸齊梁之君以行王道，惟制民恒產是急。自今視之，皆以為迂且淺，而不知道固如是也。然則四子之言，有能舉而措之，其可勝用乎？約而言之，取諸邵子，則尚行其要也；取諸程子，則定志其要也；取諸西京二子，則謹獨正心其要也。苟有會于吾心，吾擇善而從之，夫庸知四子者學之純駁與其見之淺深耶？彼固有不量其君、不察其時而强聒以進者，彼其遺恨於當時，固將有望于百千載之後耳。若其條件節目之詳、施為緩急之序，則所謂「正其本，萬事理」，未容以遽及也。

擇言之道，其博而取之，如千蹊萬徑，皆可適國，並存而無廢焉；其約而會之，如庖丁解牛，得其族則衆觧理矣。不然，吾未見其為學古訓而有獲也。漢申公有言：「為治者不在多言，顧力行何如耳。」請以是言終四子之志，執事以為何如？
translation_en:
…with the injunctions to banish the music of Zheng and keep flattering men at a distance. When Mengzi urged the rulers of Qi and Liang to practise the kingly Way, his sole pressing concern was to secure a stable livelihood for the people. Viewed from the present, these proposals are all considered impractical and shallow; yet this fails to recognize that the Way is precisely like this. If someone could take the words of the four masters and put them into practice, could their usefulness ever be exhausted? To state it briefly: in drawing upon Master Shao, the essential point is to esteem practice; in drawing upon Master Cheng, it is to make one’s resolve firm; and in drawing upon the two masters of the Western Han, it is to be watchful over oneself when alone and to rectify the mind. If something accords with my own mind, I choose what is good and follow it. Why need I concern myself with whether these four masters’ learning was pure or mixed, or their insight shallow or profound? Among them were certainly those who, without gauging their rulers or examining their times, insistently pressed their counsel upon them. Though they left behind regrets in their own day, they surely placed their hopes in the hundreds and thousands of years to come. As for the detailed provisions and particulars, and the order of urgency in putting them into effect, this is a matter of the saying, “Set the root right, and all affairs will be ordered”; we cannot hasten to address those details here.

The way to select teachings is to draw upon them broadly: like a thousand trails and ten thousand paths, all of which can lead to the capital, they may coexist without any being discarded. It is also to grasp them through their essentials: like Cook Ding cutting up an ox, once one finds the clustered joints, all the articulations fall into order. Otherwise, I have yet to see how one could study the teachings of antiquity and gain anything from them. Shen Gong of the Han said, “Governing does not depend on much talk; it depends simply on how vigorously one puts things into practice.” Allow me to conclude with these words as an expression of the aspirations of the four masters. What is your judgment, sir?

Fourth Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, School Instructor: “A vigorous and majestic spirit, expansive and learned diction, and arguments reaching to the very roots. The Six Classics are nothing other than the constant Way of our own minds. As for this Way: originating in Heaven, it is called the Mandate; endowed in human beings, it is called nature; presiding over the human person, it is called the mind. Stored within as wisdom, benevolence, sageliness, righteousness, centrality, and harmony, it is called virtue. Manifested as filial devotion, brotherly affection, concord among kin, amity among relatives by marriage, trustworthiness, and compassion, it is called conduct. Taking form in the relations between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friends, it is called the human relationships. title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
天下也之謂政推而範之天下之民使無
過不及焉之謂教合天地古今人物而無
有乎或異焉者之謂常聖人者全體乎此
心者也懼斯道之不明而或以晦焉懼斯
道之不行而或以塞焉是故取而筆之於
書以傳之天下後世俾皆由是而學焉以
得其本心故易者言乎其心之時也書者
言乎其心之中也詩者言乎其心之性情
也禮者言乎其心之序也樂者言乎其心
===
之和也春秋者言乎其心之變也故因其
時而行焉則易之道得矣即其中而施焉
則書之用昭矣約其性情而發焉則詩之
義興矣本其序而履焉則禮之理章矣由
其和而樂焉則樂之情著矣推其變而通
焉則春秋之意明矣故經也者聖人教人
以學乎其本心者也堯以是傳之舜舜以
是傳之禹禹以是傳之湯湯以是傳之文
武周公孔子而無或改焉者也火于秦黃

punctuated: 天下也之謂政。推而範之天下之民，使無過不及焉之謂教。合天地古今人物而無有乎或異焉者之謂常。聖人者，全體乎此心者也。懼斯道之不明而或以晦焉，懼斯道之不行而或以塞焉，是故取而筆之於書，以傳之天下後世，俾皆由是而學焉，以得其本心。故《易》者，言乎其心之時也；《書》者，言乎其心之中也；《詩》者，言乎其心之性情也；《禮》者，言乎其心之序也；《樂》者，言乎其心之和也；《春秋》者，言乎其心之變也。故因其時而行焉，則《易》之道得矣；即其中而施焉，則《書》之用昭矣；約其性情而發焉，則《詩》之義興矣；本其序而履焉，則《禮》之理章矣；由其和而樂焉，則《樂》之情著矣；推其變而通焉，則《春秋》之意明矣。故經也者，聖人教人以學乎其本心者也。堯以是傳之舜，舜以是傳之禹，禹以是傳之湯，湯以是傳之文武周公孔子，而無或改焉者也。火于秦，黃
translation_en: …all under Heaven: this is called government. Extending it to establish a standard for the people of all under Heaven, so that they neither exceed nor fall short of it, is called instruction. What embraces Heaven and Earth, past and present, human beings and things, without differing anywhere, is called the constant. The sage is one who fully embodies this mind. Fearing that this Way might not be understood and thus become obscured, and fearing that it might not be practiced and thus become obstructed, the sages committed it to writing to transmit it throughout the world and to later generations, so that all might study by this means and recover their original minds. Thus the Changes speaks of the mind’s responsiveness to the time; the Documents speaks of the mind’s mean; the Odes speaks of the mind’s nature and feelings; the Rites speaks of the mind’s order; the Music speaks of the mind’s harmony; and the Spring and Autumn Annals speaks of the mind’s adaptations to change. Accordingly, when one acts in accordance with the time, the Way of the Changes is attained. When one puts the mean into practice, the application of the Documents becomes clear. When one regulates one’s nature and feelings and gives them expression, the meaning of the Odes comes to life. When one bases one’s conduct on order, the principles of the Rites become manifest. When one follows harmony and takes delight in it, the true feeling of the Music becomes evident. When one extends one’s adaptations to change and responds comprehensively, the intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals becomes clear. The classics, therefore, are the means by which the sages teach people to study their original minds. Through this, Yao transmitted the teaching to Shun, Shun to Yu, Yu to Tang, and Tang to Kings Wen and Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius, without any alteration. Burned under the Qin, Huang…

title: 嘉靖十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
老于漢佛于晉宋齊梁之間而無或喪焉
者也非不能喪也心之根於人人者自不
能喪也故學者由是而學焉以得乎其本
心之正則理常矣而弗邪教貞矣而弗異
政達矣而弗悖文粹矣而弗雜道一矣而
弗二物治矣而弗亂倫若矣而弗拂行昭
矣而弗違德備矣而弗賊由是盡性以至
於命而天下之能事畢矣自夫經殘教弛
而心學不講徒求之於言語之粗而不知
===
其爲明德之實功濟之以功利之私而不
知措而爲躬行之實事是故拘之名數則
有若王弼泥之訓詁則有若鄭康成孔穎
達擬而續之則有若王仲淹因文說理則
有若蘇軾陳少南語涉空幻則有若張子
韶夫空幻妄也文詞藝也擬而續僭也訓
詁淺也名數末也五學出而六經之道晦
矣董仲舒明於春秋天人之對似矣而縱
陽閉陰之說則失之誕京房長於易學□□
